title: US History: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can sketch the American story from the first peoples to 2000 through its biggest turning points.
summary: People reached the Americas thousands of years before 1776. Six turning points (1776, 1787, 1861, 1865, 1941, 1969) and a country that grew from 13 colonies to 50 states.

cards.headline: The United States is young. The American story is not.
cards.body: People lived here for thousands of years before anyone wrote a Declaration of Independence. Here is the whole story on one page, from the first footprints to the Moon.

cards.headline: Old land, young nation
cards.body: The first Americans arrived somewhere between about 25,000 and 15,000 years ago. The United States arrived on July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. Squeeze all of that human history into a single day, and the United States shows up in the last half hour before midnight. That’s why this tree starts long before 1776.
cards.callout: People: at least 15,000 years. The United States: since 1776.

events.label: The Declaration of Independence is adopted
The Constitution is written in Philadelphia

mascot.line: Don’t memorize every date yet. Keep the order: independence, Constitution, Civil War, world war, Moon.

cards.headline: From 13 colonies to a 50th state
cards.body: The Declaration spoke for 13 British colonies breaking away from Great Britain. The Civil War later pitted the United States against 11 Southern states that tried to leave it. And the map kept growing: Hawaii became the 50th state on August 21, 1959. This tree follows that growth, and the people it swept up, from the first Americans to the end of the 20th century.

title: The First Americans
objective: After this level you can explain how people first reached the Americas from Asia during the last Ice Age, and why the timing is still debated.
summary: Ice Age seas exposed Beringia, and people crossed from East Asia, perhaps also by boat along the coast. Clovis was long thought first; Monte Verde proved otherwise, and White Sands is still debated.

cards.headline: The first Americans didn’t need a ship. They may have walked.
cards.body: During the last Ice Age, Asia and Alaska were joined by dry land. How did people get here, and when? The first answer is fairly settled. The second is still an argument.

cards.headline: A bridge made by the Ice Age
cards.body: So much of Earth’s water was frozen in glaciers that sea levels fell by as much as about 400 feet. That exposed Beringia, dry land linking Siberia and Alaska where the Bering Strait’s seafloor is now. Many scientists think people crossed from East Asia this way, following the animals they hunted. Others propose that some came by boat, along the coast. Either way, nobody set out to discover a continent. They were after dinner.

cards.headline: The Clovis-first idea
cards.body: Archaeologists kept finding one beautiful tool: a leaf-shaped, fluted stone spear point, the mark of the Clovis culture. For decades, Clovis artifacts, about 13,000 years old, were the oldest known in the Americas. So many archaeologists concluded that the Clovis people were the first Americans. It was a tidy story. Then came Chile.

mascot.line: Keep the two questions apart: the route is fairly settled; the date is the argument.

cards.headline: Older than Clovis
cards.body: At Monte Verde, a campsite in southern Chile, people were living more than 14,000 years ago, earlier than Clovis and a very long walk from Alaska. Archaeologists broadly accepted the site’s early date in 1997, and the Clovis-first idea fell. Now human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, push the story back further. Some archaeologists remain skeptical of those dates. Stay tuned.

title: A Continent of Nations
objective: After this level you can describe the variety of Native nations, languages and ways of life in North America before 1492.
summary: At European contact, North America north of Mexico spoke about 300 languages. Culture areas group its many ways of life, from Northwest Coast salmon to three sisters farms.

cards.headline: When Europeans arrived, North America spoke about 300 languages, not one.
cards.body: Each language came with its own people and way of life. Here’s how to picture that variety without memorizing a list.

cards.headline: More variety than Europe
cards.body: At European contact, North America north of Mexico had about 300 distinct languages. The linguist Edward Sapir found that the languages of California alone showed more variety than all of Europe’s. Picture a road trip up the California coast needing more phrasebooks than a grand tour of Europe.

cards.headline: Sorting a continent
cards.body: To make sense of so much variety, anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas: regions where similar ways of life occurred, such as the Northeast, the Plains, the Southwest and the Northwest Coast. Some peoples lived by hunting and gathering; others were farmers. A culture area is a map label, not a nation: each one held many different peoples.

cards.headline: Three crops, one team
cards.body: Why plant three crops in one field? In a three sisters field, corn stalks support the climbing beans, the beans add nitrogen to the soil, and the broad squash leaves shade out weeds and keep the soil moist. Each sister does a job for the others. It’s a garden with a group chat.

title: Cahokia, City of Mounds
objective: After this level you can describe Cahokia, the Mississippian city near today's St. Louis, and what its great mounds were for.
summary: Cahokia, near St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico (about 950 to 1350), perhaps bigger than London around 1100. Its earthen mounds, led by Monks Mound, held its seat of power.

cards.headline: Around 1100, a city of dirt near St. Louis probably outnumbered London.
cards.body: Not stone, not brick: earth, carried in baskets and piled into hills. Welcome to Cahokia.

cards.headline: The biggest city north of Mexico
cards.body: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest urban center north of Mexico, and it flourished from about 950 to 1350. Most of its people were farmers, and corn was the center of their farming. At its peak, around 1100, it may have held 15,000 to 20,000 people, probably a little more than London at the time. A visiting Londoner would have been the country cousin.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing, make it this: Cahokia’s biggest mound was a platform for power, built by hand.

cards.headline: A hill made by hand
cards.body: Cahokia’s mounds were built of earth carried to the site basket by basket. The biggest, Monks Mound, rises about 100 feet, and its base is about the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza’s. It is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. On top once stood a building about 100 feet long, believed to be the seat of Cahokia’s government. City hall, on a hill its people made.
cards.callout: Monks Mound: about 100 feet tall, built of earth

cards.headline: A calendar made of posts
cards.body: Cahokians also set up circles of wooden posts, now called Woodhenge. At certain times of the year the rising sun lined up with the posts, so the circles served as a calendar. No batteries, no paper, and it never ran slow.

cards.headline: Why did it empty out?
cards.body: By about 1350, Cahokia’s great days were over. The likeliest cause is environmental damage: cutting the forests brought erosion and flooding. Disease, climate change, social stress and warfare may also have played a part. Nobody left a note, so historians weigh the clues.

title: Towns in the Cliffs
objective: After this level you can explain how Ancestral Puebloans built the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde.
summary: Ancestral Puebloans built Chaco Canyon's multistory great houses from the mid-800s and Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings from about 1180 to 1300, then moved south after the Great Drought.

cards.headline: Some Americans once built apartment blocks into the side of a cliff.
cards.body: Then they moved away and left the buildings standing. Who built them, and why walk away?

cards.headline: Whose ancestors?
cards.body: The builders are called Ancestral Puebloans, because they are among the ancestors of today’s Pueblo peoples. You may still see an older name, Anasazi. It comes from Navajo, and Pueblo people consider it disrespectful. So the newer name does two jobs: it’s polite, and it tells you who the living descendants are.

cards.headline: Chaco’s great houses
cards.body: In Chaco Canyon, in today’s New Mexico, Chacoan culture flourished from the mid-800s for more than 300 years. Its builders raised great houses: massive stone buildings several stories tall with hundreds of rooms, often lined up with the sun and the moon. The largest, Pueblo Bonito, was D-shaped, four to five stories high and held over 600 rooms. Roads linked Chaco to more than 150 great houses across the region. Think of a hub with spokes.

cards.headline: Moving into the cliffs
cards.body: To the north, at Mesa Verde in today’s Colorado, people built most of their cliff dwellings between about 1180 and 1300, tucked into alcoves in the canyon walls. The biggest, Cliff Palace, is the largest cliff dwelling in North America. A home with a stone roof overhead and a very steep driveway.

mascot.line: People often say the cliff dwellers “vanished.” They didn’t. They moved south, and their descendants are the Pueblo peoples.

cards.headline: Why leave?
cards.body: By 1300, after the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299, most people had left Mesa Verde. They moved south into what is now New Mexico and Arizona. The cliff towns stayed behind, and the people who built them are among the ancestors of today’s Pueblo peoples.

title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Law of Peace joined five nations into one league, and why its influence on the US Constitution is debated.
summary: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha joined five nations under the Great Law of Peace: 50 chiefs chosen by Clan Mothers, unanimous decisions. Whether it shaped the US Constitution is still argued.

cards.headline: Five nations buried their weapons under a tree, then recorded it in beads.
cards.body: That’s the founding story of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. It is also the start of an argument about the US Constitution.

cards.headline: The People of the Longhouse
cards.body: Haudenosaunee means “People of the Longhouse.” The five original nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. Their tradition credits the Peacemaker, helped by Hiawatha, with uniting them under the Great Law of Peace. The Hiawatha Belt records the moment the warring nations buried their weapons under the Tree of Peace, in Onondaga territory. Wampum beads are white and purple shell, and a belt’s design is a memory aid for history and laws: a constitution you can hold.

cards.headline: How the League decided
cards.body: Under the Great Law, 50 peace chiefs shared authority, each nation had one vote, and decisions had to be unanimous. Each nation’s chiefs are chosen by Clan Mothers. In 1722 the Tuscarora joined, and the English began calling the league the Six Nations. Even its birthday is debated: many scholars say the 1400s, some as late as about 1600, and others argue for 1142, the year of a solar eclipse that may match a sign in the sky in the oral tradition.

cards.headline: The colonists were watching
cards.body: At a 1744 treaty meeting, the Onondaga leader Canassatego urged the colonies to unite. In 1751 Benjamin Franklin argued that if the Six Nations could form such a union, a dozen English colonies should manage one too. In 1988, on the Constitution’s 200th anniversary, Congress passed a resolution acknowledging the contribution of the Iroquois Confederacy and other Indian nations to the United States.

mascot.line: Notice the move: the events of 1744, 1751 and 1988 are settled. The argument is about what they add up to.

cards.headline: How historians weigh it
cards.body: Historians still argue about how far the influence went. Donald Grinde and Bruce Johansen argue that Iroquois and other Native political ideas helped shape American government, including the Constitution. Skeptics answer that European political theory supplied the Founders’ models and that the evidence for Native influence is thin.

title: The Columbian Exchange
objective: After this level you can explain how crops, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic after 1492, and why epidemics devastated Native peoples.
summary: After 1492, American crops spread worldwide while horses, cattle and wheat came to the Americas. Crowd diseases new to the Americas cut Native populations by 50 to 95 percent by 1650.

cards.headline: After 1492, the whole world started swapping lunches. And germs.
cards.body: Crops, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions. Some swaps fed the world. One kind was a catastrophe for Native peoples.

cards.headline: A name for the great swap
cards.body: Historians call it the Columbian Exchange: the transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world that followed Columbus’s voyage of 1492. The name comes from the historian Alfred W. Crosby’s 1972 book, which sorted the traffic into three lanes: diseases, animals and plants.

items.label: From the Americas
points: Tomatoes, peanuts, squashes, pineapples, chili peppers

cards.headline: A horse changes the Plains
cards.body: Not every arrival was a disaster. On horseback, Plains peoples could hunt bison far more successfully, boosting their food supplies until the 1870s, when the bison dwindled. One imported animal reshaped a whole way of life.

mascot.line: Keep this: Native peoples weren’t weaker. Their bodies had simply never met these germs before.

cards.headline: Germs with no warning
cards.body: The deadliest cargo was invisible. Before 1492, the Americas had none of the acute infectious diseases, such as smallpox, measles and influenza, that had long troubled Eurasia and Africa. Many came from herd animals like cattle and pigs, which the first Americans had not domesticated. So when the germs arrived, no one here had met them before. Across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, largely because of epidemics.
cards.callout: Populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650

title: Spain Comes North
objective: After this level you can explain how Spain founded St. Augustine and New Mexico, and why the Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out in 1680.
summary: Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565 and settled New Mexico from 1598. Po'pay's knotted cords coordinated the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which kept Spain out until 1692.

cards.headline: In 1680, the Pueblo peoples drove a European empire out of New Mexico.
cards.body: For twelve years, Spain stayed out. The revolt came after decades of Spanish rule in the north. First: how did Spain get there?

cards.headline: Spain gets there early
cards.body: On September 8, 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine, Florida, partly because France was trying to settle there too. It is the oldest continuously occupied city founded by Europeans in the United States. Out west, Juan de Oñate led settlers, priests and soldiers into today’s New Mexico in 1598, and Santa Fe became its capital in 1610.

cards.headline: Why the Pueblos rose
cards.body: Spanish rule pressed hard. Missionaries forced Catholicism on the Pueblo peoples and burned their kivas, masks and other sacred objects, and Pueblo people suffered forced labor and hunger. Po’pay, a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh), had himself been imprisoned and flogged by the Spanish. He planned a revolt that needed many separate pueblos to move as one.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize August 21. Remember the order: years of pressure, a secret countdown, a Spanish retreat.

cards.headline: A countdown on a string
cards.body: Po’pay’s runners carried knotted cords to the pueblos. One knot was to be untied each day until the last was gone. The Spanish caught two runners, so the Pueblos struck early: on August 10, 1680, almost all of them rose together. By August 21 the Spanish had fled south toward what is now El Paso, Texas, leaving about 400 dead, including 21 priests. A piece of string had outwitted a colonial government.

cards.headline: Twelve years
cards.body: The Pueblos stayed free until 1692, when Diego de Vargas retook New Mexico for Spain. Twelve years is short on a timeline, and very long when you are the one who is free.

title: Jamestown and the Powhatan
objective: After this level you can explain how Jamestown survived after 1607, how tobacco made it pay, and how it collided with the Powhatan chiefdom.
summary: Jamestown (1607) nearly died in the Starving Time. John Rolfe's tobacco made it pay from 1614, but its hunger for land led to war with the Powhatan chiefdom in 1622.

cards.headline: England’s first lasting colony nearly quit. A Caribbean plant saved it.
cards.body: Jamestown survived disease, starvation and a powerful neighbor. Then tobacco made it pay, and set it on a collision course with that neighbor.

cards.headline: A bad place to build
cards.body: On May 14, 1607, the Virginia Company of London founded Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in North America. The marshy site proved unhealthy: bad river water, mosquitoes and short rations brought dysentery and fevers. Moving into a swamp is rarely a good first step.

cards.headline: The powerful neighbor
cards.body: The land already had a ruler. Powhatan, whose given name was Wahunsenacawh, was paramount chief of Tsenacomoco, in tidewater Virginia. He had united dozens of tribes, more than 150 towns paid him tribute, and he was the highest authority in the region when the English built their fort.

cards.headline: The Starving Time
cards.body: In the winter of 1609 to 1610, drought, a Powhatan siege and scarce supplies left only about 60 of some 500 colonists alive at Jamestown. In June 1610 the survivors boarded ships to go home, but an incoming fleet ordered them to turn back. Jamestown was rescued on its way out the door.

cards.headline: Tobacco makes it pay
cards.body: John Rolfe replaced Virginia’s harsh native tobacco with milder plants from the West Indies. After he shipped his first barrels to England in 1614, other colonists saw his lucrative results and copied him. The colony had found its cash crop. It went up in smoke, profitably.

mascot.line: A common mix-up: Pocahontas married John Rolfe, not John Smith.

cards.headline: Peace, then war
cards.body: In April 1614 Rolfe married Powhatan’s daughter Pocahontas, and the marriage brought peace. (John Smith’s famous claim that she saved his life is doubted: some think he misunderstood a ceremony, others that he invented it.) But tobacco led settlers to press further into Native land. In 1622 Powhatan warriors led by Opechancanough, Powhatan’s brother and successor, struck back, killing 347 of about 1,200 colonists.

In the Northeast, five nations governed themselves under the Great Law of Peace. In New Mexico, the Pueblos could rise together and drive Spain out. What the newcomers carried mattered as much as who they were: across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, largely because of epidemics. The map was never blank. It was being redrawn.

title: The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag
objective: After this level you can explain why the Wampanoag allied with Plymouth, and how the harvest feast of 1621 differs from the later Thanksgiving story.
summary: An epidemic emptied Patuxet before Plymouth rose on it in 1620. Ousamequin allied with the colonists in 1621 for his own reasons; their harvest that fall was not yet Thanksgiving.

cards.headline: Why did about 90 Wampanoag men join an English colony’s harvest in 1621?
cards.body: The answer isn’t turkey. It’s an alliance, and it starts with an empty village.

cards.headline: An empty village
cards.body: Between 1616 and 1619, an epidemic ravaged the Wampanoag and their neighbors. It emptied Patuxet, the home village of a man named Tisquantum. When the Mayflower colonists founded Plymouth in 1620, they built it on the very site of Patuxet. This is Level 7’s story of new diseases, and here the germs arrived before the colonists did.

cards.headline: Ousamequin’s choice
cards.body: The epidemic left the Wampanoag exposed to the Narragansett, rivals who had escaped it. The Wampanoag leader Ousamequin, whom the English called Massasoit, saw a use for the newcomers: English guns and soldiers could help against the Narragansett. In 1621 he and Plymouth agreed to defend each other and to trade. The alliance was his strategy, not a favor.

cards.headline: The go-between
cards.body: Tisquantum, often called Squanto, had a story of his own. An English captain kidnapped him to be sold as a slave in Spain. He escaped to England and learned English, then came home in 1619 to find his people wiped out by disease. His English made him Plymouth’s interpreter. The colony’s famous helper had first been a captive.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: 1621 was a harvest shared by allies. The national holiday, and most of the story around it, came much later.

cards.headline: The harvest of 1621
cards.body: In the fall of 1621, about 90 Wampanoag men led by Ousamequin joined about 50 colonists celebrating their harvest. They stayed several days, and the Wampanoag brought venison. It is commonly called the first Thanksgiving, but Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863. Since 1970, Native people and supporters have gathered at Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day for a National Day of Mourning.

title: A City Upon a Hill
objective: After this level you can explain what the Puritans hoped to build in Massachusetts and why they banished dissenters like Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson.
summary: In 1630 Winthrop's Puritans set out to be a model "city upon a hill". Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson challenged them, were banished, and moved to what became Rhode Island.

cards.headline: The Puritans built a model society. Dissenters were shown the door.
cards.body: They believed the whole world was watching. So what happened to people who disagreed out loud?

cards.headline: A city upon a hill
cards.body: In 1630 John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, led a fleet of mostly Puritan settlers to New England. Puritans wanted a godly society and a church purified of what they saw as corruptions in the Church of England. In his sermon A Model of Christian Charity, Winthrop said the colony would be “a city upon a hill”, with all the world watching it. No pressure.

cards.headline: Roger Williams says no
cards.body: Roger Williams, a minister, argued that magistrates had no right to rule anyone’s conscience. Worse, to the colony’s leaders, he said Native people, not the king’s charter, truly owned the land. Massachusetts banished him in 1635. The Narragansett sold him land, and he founded Providence, open to people of all faiths.

cards.headline: Anne Hutchinson’s meetings
cards.body: Anne Hutchinson held weekly meetings of Boston women to discuss sermons and share her own religious views. The colony’s leaders saw a challenge to its ministers. Convicted in 1637 of slandering them, she was banished, and in 1638 she helped found a settlement on Aquidneck, an island now in Rhode Island. The city upon a hill had no room for a second preacher.

title: Thirteen Colonies, Three Regions
objective: After this level you can compare New England, the Middle Colonies and the Southern Colonies by who settled them and how they made a living.
summary: Soil and climate made three regions: New England's farms, fish and trade; the diverse, grain-rich Middle Colonies; and the South's tobacco, rice and indigo, worked by enslaved people.

cards.headline: Same king, same language, three very different ways to make a living.
cards.body: Soil and climate sorted the colonies into three regions. Tell me what grew there, and you can guess who did the work.

cards.headline: New England: rocky and salty
cards.body: New England’s rocky soil and cold winters suited small family farms, not big ones. So colonists turned to the sea and the forest: fishing, lumbering, shipbuilding and trade. If the ground won’t give you a fortune, build a boat.

cards.headline: The Middle Colonies: breadbasket
cards.body: Farther south, fertile soil grew enough wheat and other grain to export, and the Middle Colonies were called the breadbasket colonies. They drew an unusually diverse mix of settlers, including Germans and Scots-Irish as well as English. In 1681 Charles II granted the Quaker William Penn a charter for Pennsylvania, which Penn opened to settlers of many faiths.

cards.headline: The South: cash crops
cards.body: In the Chesapeake colonies of Virginia and Maryland, planters grew tobacco. In the Carolinas and Georgia, they grew rice and indigo. These plantations came to rely on the forced labor of enslaved Africans. The South’s wealth grew in its fields, and other people were made to work them.

title: How Slavery Took Root
objective: After this level you can explain how colonial laws turned slavery into a lifelong, inherited status based on race.
summary: The first recorded Africans reached Virginia in 1619 with no set status. Court rulings and laws of 1641 and 1662 made slavery lifelong, race-based and inherited.

cards.headline: Slavery in the colonies wasn’t one decision. It was built law by law.
cards.body: When the first Africans reached English Virginia, no law there said what they were. Colonial courts and lawmakers wrote the answer.

cards.headline: “20 and odd”
cards.body: In late August 1619 the English ship White Lion brought “20 and odd” Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia. Their legal status is unclear: they may have been enslaved for life, or freed after years of service. At the start, the law hadn’t yet decided.

cards.headline: A free landowner
cards.body: Some did become free. Anthony Johnson, listed as “Antonio the Negro” in 1625, gained his freedom and became a landowner among free Africans in Northampton County. In early Virginia, a free African planter was possible. The laws that came next made it much harder.

cards.headline: One crime, two sentences
cards.body: Three servants ran away together in Virginia. When they were caught, a court gave the two white men extra years of service. It sentenced the third, John Punch, an African, to serve for life. Same act, different punishment, decided by race.

cards.headline: Written into law
cards.body: In 1641 Massachusetts became the first English colony to legalize slavery, in its Body of Liberties. In 1662 Virginia made a child enslaved or free according to the mother’s status, reversing the English rule that status followed the father. Now slavery passed from mother to child, generation after generation.

title: The Middle Passage
objective: After this level you can describe the Atlantic crossing enslaved Africans were forced to endure, and how many were carried to the Americas.
summary: SlaveVoyages estimates about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard and 10.7 million survived. Equiano told of the crossing; captives revolted; about 388,000 landed in North America.

cards.headline: About 12.5 million people were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas.
cards.body: The Middle Passage was their crossing of the Atlantic. Here is what the records, and one survivor, tell us.

cards.headline: Counting a crossing
cards.body: Historians count the voyages with the SlaveVoyages database, built from shipping records. Its estimates: about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard ships to the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. The gap means roughly 1.8 million people died on the way.

cards.headline: Below deck
cards.body: Olaudah Equiano, once enslaved and later free, published an autobiography in 1789. He described captives kept below deck in chains and filth, amid “the shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying.” His book gave readers something the ship records couldn’t: a survivor’s voice.

cards.headline: Fighting back
cards.body: Captives did not simply endure. They rose in revolt on about one slave ship in ten, most often while the ship was still near the African coast. Few of the revolts succeeded, but they show that captives fought back.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize every figure. Remember the scale: millions carried, and only a small share to mainland North America.

cards.headline: Where the ships went

title: King Philip's War
objective: After this level you can explain why Metacom led New England's Native nations into war in 1675 and what the war cost both sides.
summary: Massasoit's son Metacom listed his people's grievances: lost land, cattle, unfair courts. War came in 1675, and for its size it was one of the bloodiest in American history.

cards.headline: Level 11’s alliance ended in war. The leader was Massasoit’s own son.
cards.body: Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, went to war against the colonists. His own complaints tell us why.

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 11’s alliance a generation later, strained by the colonists’ growing hunger for land.

cards.headline: Massasoit’s son
cards.body: Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, was a Wampanoag sachem, or leader, and a son of Massasoit, who had greeted Plymouth’s colonists in 1621. The father made the alliance; the son inherited what it had become.

cards.headline: In Metacom’s words
cards.body: We know Metacom’s side because a colonist wrote it down. In June 1675 he told John Easton of Rhode Island his people’s complaints: they were losing their land, English cattle were ruining their crops, and English courts treated them unfairly. It was a list of grievances, recorded just before the war began.

cards.headline: The spark and the sides
cards.body: In June 1675 Plymouth hanged three Wampanoag men for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian convert and interpreter. War followed. The Wampanoag, Nipmuc and Narragansett fought the colonists, while the Mohegan and Pequot fought alongside the English. It was never simply Native people against colonists.

cards.headline: What it cost
cards.body: Colonial forces under Benjamin Church killed Metacom in August 1676. About 600 English colonists were killed and many towns destroyed. Thousands of Native people were killed, and many were sold into slavery. For the size of the population, it was one of the bloodiest wars in American history.

title: Women in the Colonies
objective: After this level you can explain coverture and the work colonial women did, from running households to growing indigo like Eliza Lucas Pinckney.
summary: Coverture merged a wife's legal identity into her husband's, but widows could run businesses. Eliza Lucas made indigo pay, with the labor and skill of enslaved people.

cards.headline: In colonial law, a married woman almost vanished.
cards.body: Under coverture she couldn’t even sign a contract. Yet women ran households, businesses and, in one case, a new industry.

cards.headline: Covered by her husband
cards.body: Colonists brought an English legal rule called coverture. A married woman’s legal existence merged into her husband’s: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name. On paper, a wife was covered by her husband, like a letter inside an envelope.

cards.headline: Women at work
cards.body: The law didn’t stop the work. Colonial households ran on women’s labor: cooking, cleaning, spinning, weaving, sewing, and making butter and soap. And unmarried women and widows, called femes soles, could own property, make contracts and run businesses in their own names. Lose a husband, gain a legal identity.

cards.headline: A teenager and a blue dye
cards.body: Around 1739 Eliza Lucas, 16, was left to manage her father’s Wappoo Plantation near Charleston and two larger South Carolina estates. After trying crops such as ginger and cotton, she grew a successful indigo crop. Indigo became South Carolina’s second most lucrative crop, after rice.

cards.headline: Whose hands?
cards.body: The story has more people in it. In colonial South Carolina, enslaved people did almost all the work of growing indigo and turning it into dye, skilled work learned through long experience. Lucas made the plans; their labor and know-how made the blue.

title: Colonists Govern Themselves
objective: After this level you can explain how elected assemblies and town meetings gave colonists a habit of governing themselves.
summary: The House of Burgesses (1619), the Mayflower Compact (1620) and town meetings made self-rule a habit, though few could vote. Assemblies held the purse while Britain looked away.

cards.headline: The king was an ocean away. Colonists got used to running things themselves.
cards.body: Elected assemblies, town meetings and a distant king made self-rule a habit. For some colonists, anyway.

cards.headline: The first assemblies
cards.body: Virginia’s House of Burgesses first met at Jamestown on July 30, 1619, the first elected assembly in English America. The next year, before landing in 1620, 41 men aboard the Mayflower signed the Mayflower Compact, forming a “civil body politic” to make laws. Self-government came over with the first ships.

cards.headline: Town meetings, and who voted
cards.body: In New England town meetings, a town’s voters gathered to elect local officials and vote on taxes and spending. But “voters” meant a narrow group. They were usually white men who owned property; women, enslaved people and Native people were shut out. The habit of self-rule was real, and so were its limits.

cards.headline: The power of the purse
cards.body: Colonial assemblies controlled taxes and spending, including the royal governor’s salary, which they could withhold. Britain, meanwhile, enforced its rules loosely. In 1775 Edmund Burke credited the colonies’ success to this “wise and salutary neglect.” A governor who wants to get paid learns to listen.

title: The French and Indian War
objective: After this level you can explain how the war of 1754 to 1763 made Britain master of eastern North America but left it deep in debt.
summary: From 1754 to 1763 Britain and France, each with Native allies, fought for North America. Britain won Canada and the East, but its debt nearly doubled.

cards.headline: A skirmish in the Ohio woods grew into a war between empires.
cards.body: Britain won almost everything it fought for. Then it got the bill.

cards.headline: A young Virginian’s bad start
cards.body: In 1754 George Washington led Virginia troops to drive the French from the Ohio Valley. Outnumbered, he surrendered at Fort Necessity. It was the opening of the French and Indian War (1754 to 1763), the North American part of a wider war between Britain and France, the Seven Years’ War.

mascot.line: It connects: the Iroquois Confederacy is Level 6’s Haudenosaunee, the league joined by the Great Law of Peace.

cards.headline: Choosing sides
cards.body: Native nations were not bystanders. France fought with many Native allies, such as the Shawnee, while Britain’s main Native partner was the Iroquois Confederacy.

cards.headline: A plan for union
cards.body: At Albany in 1754, Benjamin Franklin proposed uniting the colonies under one council. The colonial assemblies and the Crown rejected it. The colonies would not yet act as one.

cards.headline: Winning big, owing big
cards.body: In the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Britain gained Canada and France’s lands east of the Mississippi except New Orleans, and Florida from Spain. But the war nearly doubled Britain’s national debt, and Britain expected the colonies to help pay it off. In 1763, Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley attacked British forts in Pontiac’s War, and Britain then barred colonists from settling farther west.

title: The Stamp Act Crisis
objective: After this level you can explain why the Stamp Act of 1765 set off the cry "no taxation without representation", and what Parliament argued back.
summary: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed colonial paper. Colonists said only their own representatives could tax them; Parliament answered with virtual representation.

cards.headline: A tax on paper set thirteen colonies arguing.
cards.body: In 1765 Parliament taxed the colonists’ newspapers, contracts and playing cards. The money was not the real fight. The fight was over who had the right to tax them at all.

cards.headline: A stamp on everything
cards.body: After the French and Indian War, Britain faced heavy costs to defend its American colonies, and it wanted the colonists to help pay. Its answer was the Stamp Act of 1765. Legal papers, newspapers, pamphlets, playing cards and even dice had to carry a stamp showing the tax was paid. Picture paying the government a fee every time you bought a paper or signed a lease.

cards.headline: No taxation without representation
cards.body: Colonists argued that free people could be taxed only with their own consent, given through their own representatives, and no colonist sat in Parliament. The Sons of Liberty, formed in the summer of 1765, went further: they destroyed the stamps wherever they found them.

cards.headline: Parliament’s answer: virtual representation
cards.body: British writers replied that the colonists were represented already. Whole English cities, like Manchester, elected no member of Parliament, yet every member was supposed to speak for the entire nation. If that worked for Manchester, why not Boston? Colonists rejected the idea: a Parliament they had never elected could not consent to taxes for them.

cards.headline: Boycott, repeal and a warning
cards.body: Delegates from nine colonies met in New York in October 1765 as the Stamp Act Congress and petitioned against the tax. Colonists also boycotted British goods, and British merchants, watching their sales fall, pressed Parliament to back down. On March 18, 1766, it repealed the Stamp Act. The same day it passed the Declaratory Act, claiming power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The tax was gone. The argument was not.

title: From Massacre to Tea Party
objective: After this level you can trace how the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts pushed Britain and the colonies toward war.
summary: Townshend duties, troops in Boston, the Massacre of 1770 and the Tea Party of 1773 led to the Intolerable Acts of 1774, which united the colonies.

cards.headline: Every British move got an answer, and every answer raised the stakes.
cards.body: Between 1767 and 1774, Boston went from protests to shootings to a harbor full of tea. Follow the chain.

cards.headline: New taxes, new troops
cards.body: In 1767 the Townshend Acts put duties on lead, glass, paper, paint and tea imported into the colonies. Boston resisted, and in October 1768 two British regiments arrived to keep order. Now soldiers lived among the people they were policing: a recipe for trouble.

cards.headline: The Boston Massacre
cards.body: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five colonists. Among the first to fall was Crispus Attucks, a Black sailor who had likely been enslaved. John Adams, a patriot lawyer, defended the soldiers in court, arguing they had a right to defend themselves. Six of the eight were acquitted.

cards.headline: Tea in the harbor
cards.body: The Tea Act of 1773 let the East India Company sell tea more cheaply in the colonies, but the tax on tea stayed. Cheaper tea, same principle. On December 16, 1773, men disguised as Native Americans boarded ships in Boston Harbor and dumped about 340 chests of tea overboard.

mascot.line: Keep this: each crackdown meant for Boston pulled more colonies onto Boston’s side.

cards.headline: Punish Boston, unite the colonies
cards.body: In 1774 Parliament closed Boston’s port until the tea was paid for and replaced Massachusetts’ elected council with an appointed one. Colonists called these the Intolerable Acts. The punishment backfired: on September 5, 1774, delegates from every colony but Georgia met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress and called for a boycott of British goods.

title: Lexington and Concord

cards.headline: The shooting started on a village green at dawn.
cards.body: On April 19, 1775, British regulars met colonial militia at Lexington. Why were farmers ready to fight at a moment’s notice?

cards.headline: Ready in a minute
cards.body: In 1774 Massachusetts patriots set up their own Provincial Congress. It took control of the colony’s militia and stockpiled arms, ammunition and provisions. In October 1774 it urged towns to raise minutemen: volunteers who trained and would be ready at a minute’s notice. The colony was preparing for a fight before anyone fired a shot.

mascot.line: A common mix-up: Paul Revere wasn’t a lone rider. William Dawes and Samuel Prescott carried the alarm too.

cards.headline: The midnight warning
cards.body: General Thomas Gage ordered British troops to march from Boston and seize the colonists’ military stores at Concord. The patriots had planned for this. Prearranged lantern signals showed whether the troops went by water or by land, and riders set off to spread the alarm.

cards.headline: Lexington, then Concord
cards.body: At dawn on April 19, 1775, British regulars faced militia on Lexington’s green. The British volley killed 8 militiamen and wounded 10. At Concord’s North Bridge, the militia fired on a British party and forced it to pull back.

cards.headline: A long road back
cards.body: The march back to Boston was an ordeal. Militia fired on the British from behind houses, barns, trees and stone walls along the road. Then thousands of New Englanders gathered around Boston and besieged it. The argument had become a war.

title: Common Sense
objective: After this level you can explain how Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet turned many colonists from protest toward independence.
summary: Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (January 1776) argued in plain words against kings and for independence, and was read aloud far beyond its buyers.

cards.headline: What turns a protest into a revolution? Sometimes, a pamphlet.
cards.body: In January 1776 a newcomer from England published the most talked-about argument in America.

cards.headline: A newcomer with a pen
cards.body: Thomas Paine came to the colonies from England in November 1774, carrying letters of introduction from Benjamin Franklin. On January 10, 1776, he published Common Sense. It didn’t ask for fairer taxes. It argued for independence, and against having a king at all.

cards.headline: Plain words, big ideas
cards.body: Paine wrote in plain language for ordinary readers. He attacked hereditary rule: no one, he said, had a right by birth to set his family above everyone else. And he mocked the empire’s very shape: “there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.”

cards.headline: Heard, not just read
cards.body: Common Sense was short enough to read aloud, and people read it in taverns and on street corners to listeners who could not read. One copy could reach a whole room. It is often called America’s first best-seller.

cards.headline: How many copies?
cards.body: Paine claimed that about 120,000 copies sold in three months. Historian Trish Loughran tested the boast: counting 25 printings of at most 3,000 copies each, she puts the upper limit near 75,000. Big or merely large, Paine’s own number is a claim to weigh, not a fact to repeat.

title: The Declaration of Independence
objective: After this level you can explain the Declaration's argument about rights and consent, and the contradiction with slavery that critics pointed out at the time.
summary: The Declaration of Independence argued for equal rights and government by consent, while its author enslaved people, a contradiction critics named at once.

cards.headline: “All men are created equal,” wrote a man who enslaved hundreds.
cards.body: The Declaration of 1776 changed how the world talks about rights. Critics pointed at its contradiction right away.

mascot.line: A common mix-up: the vote for independence came on July 2. July 4 is when Congress adopted the Declaration.

cards.headline: Five men, one writer
cards.body: In June 1776 Congress chose Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston to draft a declaration. Jefferson wrote the draft. On July 2 Congress voted that the colonies were “free and independent states,” and on July 4, 1776, it adopted the Declaration.

cards.headline: The argument
cards.body: “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.” Governments, it continues, derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed,” and when one destroys people’s rights, they may “alter or to abolish it.” Most of the rest is a charge sheet: a long list of grievances accusing King George III of “repeated injuries and usurpations.”

cards.headline: What Congress cut
cards.body: Jefferson’s draft blamed the king for the slave trade, calling it “cruel war against human nature itself.” Congress struck the passage out; Jefferson later said it was cut to please South Carolina and Georgia. Jefferson himself enslaved more than 600 people over his lifetime.

cards.headline: Critics at the time
cards.body: In 1775 the British writer Samuel Johnson had already asked: “How is it that we hear the loudest yelps for liberty among the drivers of negroes?” Black Americans made the point themselves. In January 1777, Prince Hall and seven other Black men petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for freedom, as the natural right of all people.

title: How the Colonies Won
objective: After this level you can explain how Saratoga, the French alliance and Yorktown let an outmatched army win independence.
summary: Burgoyne’s surrender at Saratoga (1777) won the French alliance; French troops and a French fleet trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown (1781).

cards.headline: Two British armies surrendered, in 1777 and 1781. What changed in between?
cards.body: The answer has a French accent.

cards.headline: Saratoga
cards.body: In 1777 a British army under General John Burgoyne pushed into upstate New York. It never got out. On October 17, 1777, near Saratoga, Burgoyne surrendered his whole army to American General Horatio Gates.

cards.headline: A powerful friend
cards.body: France had already been sending the Americans aid in secret through agents. News of Saratoga persuaded France’s foreign minister, the comte de Vergennes, to choose an open alliance. On February 6, 1778, Benjamin Franklin and two other envoys signed a Treaty of Alliance with France, and Spain entered the war against Britain in 1779.

cards.headline: Trapped at Yorktown
cards.body: In 1781 Washington and the French general Rochambeau marched their armies south and trapped General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia. A French fleet under the comte de Grasse controlled the sea, so no British ships could rescue him. On October 19, 1781, Cornwallis surrendered, and the major fighting of the Revolution was over.

cards.headline: Peace, with help
cards.body: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 formally ended the war between Britain and the United States, France and Spain. The State Department’s own historians call French help crucial to the victory at Yorktown. The Americans won independence, with a great deal of help from France.

title: Loyalists and Native Nations
objective: After this level you can explain why many colonists stayed loyal to Britain and why most Native nations sided with the Crown.
summary: Loyalists, perhaps 15 percent to a third of colonists, sided with the Crown; most Native nations that fought did too, hoping to keep their lands.

cards.headline: Not every American wanted independence.
cards.body: Neighbors split, families split, and an old league of Native nations split too. Who stood by the king, and why?

cards.headline: Who stayed loyal
cards.body: Loyalists came from every colony: royal officeholders, Anglican clergy and their congregations, large landholders, wealthy merchants, and pacifist Quakers. What most shared was a cautious, conservative streak and a deep devotion to Britain and the Crown. Estimates of their numbers range from about 15 percent of colonists to about a third.

cards.headline: The price of losing
cards.body: When the war ended, many Loyalists left for good. Estimates range from about 60,000 to 100,000 people. Most went to Canada, to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec.

cards.headline: Why Native nations chose Britain
cards.body: Most Native nations that fought sided with Britain, from old alliances and a belief that they had a better chance of keeping their lands under the British. The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) led Haudenosaunee fighters allied with the British in raids on New York and Pennsylvania settlements.

cards.headline: A league divided
cards.body: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy first tried to stay neutral, then split. The Oneida and Tuscarora backed the Americans; most other nations backed Britain. Oneida allies carried corn to Washington’s starving army at Valley Forge, and an Oneida woman, Polly Cooper, stayed to show soldiers how to cook it.

cards.headline: Left out of the peace
cards.body: In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, neither Britain nor the United States made any provision for their Six Nations allies. Friends and enemies of the Americans alike were left to negotiate on their own.

title: Liberty and Slavery in the War
objective: After this level you can explain how enslaved people sought freedom on both sides of the war, and why northern states began to end slavery.
summary: Enslaved people sought freedom on both sides of the war; Massachusetts courts and a Pennsylvania law of 1780 began ending slavery in the North.

cards.headline: In a war about liberty, enslaved people had the most at stake.
cards.body: Some ran to the British, some fought for the Americans, and some went to court.

cards.headline: The British offer
cards.body: In November 1775 Lord Dunmore, Virginia’s royal governor, promised freedom to servants and enslaved people of rebels who would bear arms for the British. It was aimed at the rebels: people enslaved by Loyalists were left out. Thousands of enslaved people escaped to British lines during the war.

cards.headline: Fighting for the Americans
cards.body: Washington at first barred most Black men from enlisting in the Continental Army, then relented after Dunmore’s offer. In 1778 Rhode Island promised freedom to enslaved men who enlisted in its 1st Rhode Island Regiment. Freedom was on offer from both sides, but only for some.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 25’s “all men are created equal” was words on paper. Mum Bett took the idea to court.

cards.headline: Suing for freedom
cards.body: Massachusetts’ new constitution of 1780 declared all men born free and equal. In 1781 an enslaved woman called Mum Bett sued under it. A jury freed her, and she took the name Elizabeth Freeman. By 1783 Massachusetts’ courts had ruled that slavery could not stand there.

cards.headline: The North begins to end slavery
cards.body: Pennsylvania passed the first gradual abolition law on March 1, 1780. It freed no one at once: children later born to enslaved mothers became free at age 28. Its lawmakers wrote that their own escape from British tyranny obliged them to extend freedom to others. Other northern states passed abolition laws between 1780 and 1804.

title: Women and the Revolution
objective: After this level you can describe the parts women played, from boycotts and camp work to Abigail Adams asking her husband to "remember the ladies".
summary: Women boycotted and spun homespun, followed the armies, and sometimes fought; Abigail Adams asked the lawmakers to "remember the ladies".

cards.headline: The Revolution was fought at spinning wheels and campfires too.
cards.body: Women boycotted, cooked, nursed and sometimes fought. One asked the men writing the new laws a pointed question.

cards.headline: Spinning as protest
cards.body: During the Stamp Act crisis, women formed the Daughters of Liberty. They gave up tea and gathered for spinning bees, making homespun cloth so their families didn’t need British imports. A boycott only works if someone makes the substitute.

cards.headline: Following the army
cards.body: Thousands of women, often soldiers’ wives, daughters or mothers, traveled with the armies as camp followers. They cooked, washed, sewed and nursed the sick and wounded. An army marches on clean shirts too.

cards.headline: In uniform
cards.body: A few women fought. In 1782 Deborah Sampson disguised herself as a man and enlisted in the 4th Massachusetts Regiment. Her secret held until she fell ill and a doctor discovered it.

cards.headline: Remember the ladies
cards.body: In March 1776 Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John in Congress: “I desire you would Remember the Ladies.” Women, she warned, would not feel bound by laws “in which we have no voice, or Representation.” It was the colonists’ own argument, turned on the men making it.

cards.headline: A brief vote
cards.body: One state went further, for a while. New Jersey’s 1776 constitution let property-holding inhabitants vote, and unmarried women and widows who qualified did. An 1807 law limited voting to free white men.

title: Why the Articles Failed
objective: After this level you can explain why the Articles of Confederation left the new nation weak, and why Shays' Rebellion alarmed its leaders.
summary: The Articles of Confederation gave each state one vote and let Congress only ask for money. Shays’ Rebellion in 1786 and 1787 convinced many leaders to build a stronger government.

cards.headline: America’s first national government couldn’t make anyone pay its bills.
cards.body: Its Congress could only ask the states for money. Then, in 1786, armed farmers in Massachusetts started shutting down the courts.

cards.headline: A Congress that could only ask
cards.body: The Articles of Confederation were adopted by Congress in November 1777, but the states didn’t finish ratifying them until March 1, 1781. They created a Congress where each state had one vote. Congress could request money and troops from the states, but it had no power to make them pay. Picture a club that can send out dues reminders but can’t collect a cent.

mascot.line: Keep this: one vote per state, no power to make states pay, and no change without every state. That’s the whole problem.

cards.headline: Repairs needed everyone
cards.body: Fixing the Articles was just as hard. Any change had to be agreed in Congress and then confirmed by the legislatures of every state. A single holdout could block a repair that everyone else wanted.

cards.headline: Farmers close the courts
cards.body: In 1786, armed bands in Massachusetts protesting high taxes and hard times forced courts to close, to stop foreclosures and debt cases. Most were farmers in the western part of the state, many of them Revolutionary War veterans. In January 1787, Daniel Shays led an attack on the federal arsenal at Springfield. It was driven back, and militia routed the rebels at Petersham in February.

cards.headline: Two ways to see it
cards.body: To the rebels, this was a stand against crushing new taxes. To many leaders, the weak national response proved the country needed a stronger central government. That conviction fed the movement for a convention, and in the summer of 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia to write the Constitution.

title: The Summer of 1787
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Compromise settled the fight between large and small states at the Constitutional Convention.
summary: At the Constitutional Convention of 1787, big states wanted representation by population and small states wanted equal votes. The Great Compromise gave them both, by one vote.

cards.headline: In July 1787, the Constitution nearly died over one question.
cards.body: Should a big state count for more than a small one? The answer passed by a single vote.

cards.headline: A summer in Philadelphia
cards.body: From May 25 to September 17, 1787, delegates met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia. 55 took part; Rhode Island sent no one. They elected George Washington to preside. Remember Level 31: they had come to fix a government whose Congress could only ask the states for money.

cards.headline: Big states, small states
cards.body: Virginia’s plan, offered by Edmund Randolph, called for a two-house Congress with each state represented by its population or wealth. That suited big states. William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan answered with equal representation for every state, which suited small ones. Under the Articles, each state had one vote, and small states weren’t eager to give that up.

cards.headline: Split the difference
cards.body: Connecticut’s Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth gave their name to the fix: seats in the House by population, and equal seats for every state in the Senate. The convention adopted this Great Compromise on July 16, 1787, by one vote. Every time you hear that each state has two senators, you’re hearing the echo of that summer.

title: Slavery in the Constitution
objective: After this level you can explain the three-fifths, slave trade and fugitive clauses, and how later Americans argued over what they meant.
summary: The Constitution never names slavery, yet three clauses protected it. Garrison called it a covenant with death; after 1851 Douglass argued it could be used to end slavery.

cards.headline: The words “slave” and “slavery” never appear in the original Constitution.
cards.body: Yet slavery shaped at least three of its clauses. Americans later fought bitterly over what that silence meant.

cards.headline: Counting three-fifths
cards.body: Level 32’s Great Compromise tied House seats to population, which raised a hard question: did enslaved people count? The Constitution counted three-fifths of the enslaved population when dividing House seats and direct taxes among the states. It called them “all other Persons.” The document counted them, but never named them.

cards.headline: Two more clauses
cards.body: Two other clauses dealt with slavery without naming it. One barred Congress from banning the importation of enslaved people before 1808. The other said a person “held to Service or Labour” who escaped to another state must be “delivered up on Claim.” Crossing a state line did not end the chase.

cards.headline: A covenant with death?
cards.body: Many abolitionists read these clauses as proof that the Constitution protected slavery. On July 4, 1854, at a rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, William Lloyd Garrison burned a copy and called it “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.”

mascot.line: Notice the move: the clauses themselves are settled fact. The argument was over what they meant.

cards.headline: Or a tool for freedom?
cards.body: Frederick Douglass once shared Garrison’s view. In 1851 he broke with him, arguing that the Constitution was a valid legal document that could be used for emancipation. Its words never named slavery, he argued, so they should be read in favor of liberty, not the framers’ hopes. Same document, opposite readings.

title: The Fight Over Ratification
objective: After this level you can compare the Federalists' and Anti-Federalists' arguments, and explain how their fight produced the Bill of Rights.
summary: Federalists wrote The Federalist to win ratification; Anti-Federalists feared a distant national government with no bill of rights. Their fight produced the Bill of Rights in 1791.

cards.headline: The Constitution’s fiercest critics ended up improving it.
cards.body: Opponents said it lacked a bill of rights. Supporters said it didn’t need one. Their fight produced the first 10 amendments.

cards.headline: The case for
cards.body: Supporters of the Constitution called themselves Federalists. To win over New York, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote The Federalist: 85 essays printed in New York newspapers from October 1787 to May 1788. They were newspaper columns long before they were a classic.

cards.headline: The case against
cards.body: Anti-Federalists, including Patrick Henry, feared the plan. A single national government, they warned, could bring upper-class dominance, weak separation of powers and the loss of local control. George Mason, a delegate to the convention itself, refused to sign because the Constitution lacked a bill of rights.

cards.headline: A deal in Massachusetts
cards.body: Federalists first argued a bill of rights was unnecessary: the new government could use only the powers the Constitution listed. But with ratification in danger in Massachusetts, they agreed that the First Congress would consider amendments proposed by the states. That promise secured ratification there.

cards.headline: The losers write a chapter
cards.body: James Madison, who had once opposed a bill of rights, introduced a list of amendments in the First Congress on June 8, 1789. Congress proposed 12, and by December 15, 1791, the states had ratified 10: the Bill of Rights. The Anti-Federalists lost the fight, but their agitation added the Bill of Rights.

cards.headline: The first everything
cards.body: George Washington is the only president elected unanimously by the Electoral College, in both 1789 and 1792. With no one before him, every choice set a pattern. One of the most lasting was creating the president’s cabinet.

cards.headline: No royal titles
cards.body: The Senate proposed calling him “His Highness the President of the United States of America and Protector of their Liberties.” The House rejected any title, and the Senate gave way. A plain title suited a republic.

cards.headline: Knowing when to leave
cards.body: Washington retired after two terms, a precedent every president followed until Franklin D. Roosevelt. In his Farewell Address of 1796, he warned against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.” Walking away from power was itself the lesson.

cards.headline: Ona Judge’s own precedent

She had learned Martha Washington planned to give her to a granddaughter. Washington tried to have her recaptured, but she lived the rest of her life in New Hampshire, legally still a fugitive, until her death in 1848.

title: Hamilton, Jefferson and Parties
objective: After this level you can explain how Hamilton and Jefferson clashed over a national bank and the country's future, and how the first parties grew from it.
summary: Hamilton’s national bank set Jefferson’s strict reading of the Constitution against Hamilton’s implied powers. The quarrel over the bank and the country’s future produced the first parties.

cards.headline: Two advisers fought over a bank. Their quarrel created America’s first parties.
cards.body: Jefferson warned of “a boundless field of power.” Hamilton said the Constitution allowed it. Both had a point to make about the country’s future.

cards.headline: Hamilton’s bank
cards.body: Alexander Hamilton, the first secretary of the Treasury, urged Congress to create a national bank. After Congress passed a bank bill in February 1791, Washington asked his cabinet, including Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Hamilton himself, whether it was constitutional.

cards.headline: Listed powers or implied ones?
cards.body: Jefferson argued the Constitution gave Congress no power to create corporations, including a bank. Going beyond the listed powers, he warned, would be “to take possession of a boundless field of power.” Hamilton answered that implied powers counted as fully as listed ones: Congress could charter a bank as a means of carrying out powers it clearly had.

cards.headline: Two pictures of America
cards.body: Behind the legal fight were two visions. Jefferson pictured a mainly agrarian country and feared the bank would favor financiers and merchants over plantation owners and family farmers. Hamilton won this round: Washington signed the bill in February 1791, and the bank opened with a 20-year charter.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Jefferson’s Republicans are not today’s Republican Party. Same word, different party, two centuries apart.

cards.headline: Parties are born
cards.body: The quarrel spread. Jefferson’s supporters, favoring states’ rights and a strict reading of the Constitution, organized in 1792 as the Republican Party, later called the Democratic-Republicans. Hamilton’s Federalists favored a strong central government and a loose reading. Republicans charged that the Federalists had aristocratic attitudes and favored the wealthy.

title: The Election of 1800
objective: After this level you can explain why the first handover of power between rival parties, after a deadlocked election, mattered so much.
summary: In 1800 Jefferson and his own running mate tied at 73 electoral votes; the House chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot. Power then passed peacefully between rival parties for the first time.

cards.headline: In 1800 the young republic faced a test: would the losers hand over power?
cards.body: First it had to work out who had won. Jefferson and his own running mate tied at 73 electoral votes.

cards.headline: A tie with a teammate
cards.body: The Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson defeated the Federalist president, John Adams. But electors cast two votes without marking which was for president, so Jefferson and his running mate, Aaron Burr, each received 73 electoral votes. Imagine a team sheet that lists two names and never says which one is the captain.

cards.headline: Thirty-six tries
cards.body: The tie went to the House of Representatives, and it deadlocked. Alexander Hamilton, though a Federalist, worked against Burr and helped build support for Jefferson. On February 17, 1801, on the 36th ballot, the House chose Jefferson. To prevent a repeat, the 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804, gave president and vice president separate electoral votes.

cards.headline: Power changes hands
cards.body: The bigger news was what didn’t happen. The election of 1800 was the first in which power passed peacefully from one party to another. In his inaugural address on March 4, 1801, Jefferson reached out to the losers: “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” Rivals could fight hard and still share one country.

title: The Louisiana Purchase
objective: After this level you can explain how the 1803 purchase doubled the country, and what Lewis, Clark and Sacagawea found in lands that were already home to many nations.
summary: In 1803 the US bought France’s claim to Louisiana, doubling the country on land still home to Native nations. Sacagawea’s Shoshone kin helped Lewis and Clark cross the mountains.

cards.body: France sold its claim. The Native nations who actually lived on the land hadn’t sold anything.

cards.headline: The biggest deal
cards.body: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana territory from France for $15 million: about 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains. It doubled the size of the country. Jefferson, who read the Constitution strictly, doubted it even allowed him to buy territory. He bought it anyway.

cards.headline: What was really bought
cards.body: Maps colored it American, but the land was still largely occupied by Native peoples. The purchase gave the United States France’s imperial claim: the sole right to obtain the land from its inhabitants, by treaty or by conquest. Buying the right to make an offer on a house doesn’t move out the family living in it.

cards.headline: Sacagawea’s road
cards.body: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery through the new lands from 1804 to 1806. At the Mandan and Hidatsa villages they met Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman captured about 1800 by a Hidatsa raiding party. In the spring of 1805 she set out with the Corps, with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau and her baby son, Jean Baptiste, born that February.

cards.headline: Horses from a brother
cards.body: In August 1805 the Corps met a Shoshone band led by Sacagawea’s brother, Cameahwait. The reunion helped Lewis and Clark get the horses they needed to cross the mountains. She is often called a guide, but her biggest gifts were language and trust: she translated with the Shoshone, and her presence signaled peaceful intentions to the nations they met.

title: The War of 1812
objective: After this level you can explain why the US fought Britain again in 1812 and how the war ended Tecumseh's hope of a Native confederacy.
summary: Impressment, trade limits and British aid to Native resistance led to war in 1812. Tecumseh’s alliance fought beside Britain; he died in 1813, and the 1814 peace restored old borders.

cards.headline: Why fight Britain again?
cards.body: President James Madison signed a declaration of war against Britain on June 18, 1812. Americans had three big complaints: impressment, the Royal Navy’s practice of forcing American sailors into its service; British trade restrictions; and British support for Native resistance on the frontier.

cards.headline: Tecumseh’s alliance
cards.body: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh had his own aims. He urged Native nations from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico to set aside rivalries and unite to protect their cultures and lands. His younger brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, gave the movement spiritual backing, and in 1808 they founded Prophetstown on the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers. In November 1811, William Henry Harrison’s force destroyed it at the Battle of Tippecanoe.

cards.headline: An ally who fell
cards.body: When war came, Tecumseh allied with the British, and General Isaac Brock placed him in command of all Native forces. On October 5, 1813, he was killed at the Battle of the Thames, and his dream of a unified Native homeland never came to be.

mascot.line: Keep this: a draw between the US and Britain was still a defeat for the Native nations caught between them.

cards.headline: Who won?

title: The Trail of Tears
objective: After this level you can explain the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and how the Cherokee won in court but still lost their homeland.
summary: The Cherokee built a nation with its own writing, constitution and newspaper. They won in the Supreme Court in 1832, but Georgia and Jackson ignored the ruling, and in 1838 the army forced them west.

cards.headline: The Cherokee sued Georgia and won. Then they lost their homeland.
cards.body: How do you win in court and still lose everything? The answer runs through a new law, a disputed treaty and a long, forced walk west.

cards.headline: A nation with its own alphabet
cards.body: By 1821 Sequoyah had created a Cherokee writing system of 86 symbols, one for each syllable, and literacy spread quickly. In 1827 the Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution. In 1828 it began printing the Cherokee Phoenix, a Native nation’s first newspaper. The Cherokee were doing everything a young republic does. Their neighbors in Georgia wanted the land anyway.

mascot.line: Keep this: the Cherokee won their case. They lost their land because nobody with power enforced the ruling.

cards.headline: Winning in court
cards.body: In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, pressing Native nations of the Southeast to give up their lands for territory west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee answered with lawyers. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community where Georgia’s laws had no force. Georgia ignored the ruling, and President Andrew Jackson declined to enforce it. A court can decide. Someone else has to act.

cards.headline: A treaty most Cherokee rejected
cards.body: In late 1835 a small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up Cherokee land in the East. None of the signers were elected officials of the Cherokee Nation, and most Cherokee opposed it. The US Senate ratified it anyway in 1836.

cards.headline: The Trail of Tears
cards.body: In 1838 US soldiers and state militia forced more than 16,000 Cherokee from their homes into camps, then west to Indian Territory, today’s Oklahoma. Elizur Butler, a missionary doctor who traveled with them, estimated that over 4,000 died, nearly a fifth of the nation. The Choctaw, Muscogee Creek, Seminole and Chickasaw were removed too. In the West, the Cherokee rebuilt their nation, which remains an independent tribe.

title: Mills, Canals and Newcomers
objective: After this level you can explain how factories, canals and Irish and German immigrants transformed the North before 1860.
summary: The Erie Canal (1825) opened the interior. Lowell’s mill girls struck in 1834 and 1836. Famine sent the Irish, and Catholic newcomers met the Know-Nothings.

cards.headline: Before the Civil War, a canal, a mill town and a famine remade the North.
cards.body: A ditch across New York, factories full of farm daughters, and ships full of Irish and German newcomers. Here is how the North changed, and who pushed back.

cards.headline: The ditch that built a city
cards.body: The Erie Canal, finished in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to New York City by way of the Hudson River at Albany. Boats could now carry people and goods between the interior and the coast. The canal opened the interior of the continent to settlement and made New York City the nation’s leading commercial center. A ditch became a highway.

cards.headline: The mill girls of Lowell
cards.body: Lowell’s textile companies recruited young women, generally 15 to 30, from New England farms that offered them few chances. The draw was monthly cash wages. The price: 12 to 14 hours a day and company boardinghouses with curfews. In 1834 and 1836 the women walked out in strikes they called turnouts, against a wage cut and then higher board charges.

cards.headline: Newcomers from Ireland
cards.body: In 1845 a blight struck Ireland’s potatoes. About one million people died in the Great Famine, and perhaps 2 million more emigrated. Most Irish who came to America settled in the cities where they landed, almost all in the Northeast. Germans came in large numbers too.

cards.headline: The Know-Nothings
cards.body: Most of the Irish and many Germans were Roman Catholic, and that fed a backlash. In the 1850s the anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Know-Nothing party flourished. The name came from its members’ instructions: asked about the movement, say you know nothing. It wanted immigrants to wait 21 years before becoming citizens.

title: King Cotton
objective: After this level you can explain how the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade spread slavery across the Deep South.
summary: Whitney’s 1793 gin made inland cotton profitable and raised demand for enslaved labor. After 1808, about a million people or more were forced to the Deep South.

cards.headline: A machine built to save labor ended up spreading slavery.
cards.body: In 1793 Eli Whitney built a machine to clean cotton. Over the next decades cotton took over the South, and slavery moved with it. How did a labor-saving machine do that?

cards.headline: The sticky-seed problem
cards.body: Long-staple cotton, whose seeds come out easily, grew only near the coast. The cotton that grew inland had sticky seeds that were slow to pick out by hand. Whitney’s gin (1793) pulled the fiber through wire teeth on a turning cylinder, leaving the seeds behind. Suddenly, inland cotton was worth growing almost anywhere in the South.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the gin saved work at one step. Planting and picking still took people, so slavery grew.

cards.headline: Why the gin spread slavery
cards.body: The gin sped up one step, cleaning. Someone still had to plant, hoe and pick every boll. Cotton became so profitable that enslavers demanded more land and more enslaved people to work it. A machine that saved labor at the gin multiplied forced labor in the fields.

cards.headline: Sold south
cards.body: In 1808 Congress banned bringing enslaved people from Africa. Enslavers turned to a trade inside the country. About a million enslaved people, perhaps more, were forced from the Upper South, places like Virginia and Maryland, to cotton plantations in the Deep South. Many were marched in chained gangs, and sales split spouses, parents and children.

title: Life Under Slavery
objective: After this level you can describe the work, family life, faith and culture that enslaved people built under slavery.
summary: The law gave enslaved people almost nothing, yet they built families, faith and music: marriages honored by their communities, secret worship in hush harbors, and spirituals with double meanings.

cards.headline: What do people build when the law gives them nothing?
cards.body: Enslaved people could not legally marry, and many were told that obedience was their religious duty. Here is what they built anyway, often in secret.

cards.headline: Marriages the law ignored
cards.body: Southern laws refused to recognize marriages between enslaved people, and enslavers often separated spouses by sale. Enslaved communities took marriage seriously anyway. Some couples jumped the broom, a ritual that made a marriage real in the eyes of the community when the law would not. A wedding was an act of defiance with a party attached.

cards.headline: Church in the woods
cards.body: Preachers approved by enslavers often taught that obedience to your master was the highest religious duty. Enslaved believers built their own faith instead. Using signals and passwords whites could not read, they called one another to secret worship in the woods, called hush harbors. There they mixed African rhythms, singing and beliefs with evangelical Christianity.

cards.headline: Songs with two meanings
cards.body: Spirituals were religious folksongs created by enslaved people in the South. They were passed on only by ear, one generation to the next, and sung in call and response between a leader and a chorus. Many carried a double meaning: salvation in the next world, and freedom from slavery in this one. A song anyone could overhear could still say two things at once.
