title: Resisting Slavery
objective: After this level you can explain the ways enslaved people resisted, from slowing work and escaping to Nat Turner's revolt and the Underground Railroad.
summary: Enslaved people resisted daily, rose with Nat Turner in 1831, and escaped, often alone. The Underground Railroad and Harriet Tubman’s about 13 trips helped others.

cards.headline: Resistance didn’t start with a lantern in the window. It started in the fields.
cards.body: Enslaved people resisted slavery in small ways every day, in rare revolts, and by walking away. Here are all three.

cards.headline: Everyday resistance
cards.body: Some enslaved people slowed down work, pretended to be sick or broke tools. Each act was small, and each cost an enslaver time and money. It was resistance an overseer could never quite prove.

cards.headline: Nat Turner’s revolt
cards.body: In August 1831, in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner led a revolt in which at least 55 white people were killed. Whites then killed at least 100 Black people, many with no part in it, and Turner was hanged. Southern lawmakers answered with new laws banning the education, movement and assembly of enslaved people.

cards.headline: The Underground Railroad
cards.body: Many freedom seekers escaped on their own, without help. Over time, helpers of all races built a secret network, and it borrowed railway words: safe houses were stations and guides were conductors. Freedom seekers headed not only north but to Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida and beyond.

cards.headline: Harriet Tubman, conductor
cards.body: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 when she was about to be sold. Then she went back, about 13 times, to rescue family and friends, and she later said she never lost a passenger. An 1868 biography inflated her record to about 19 trips and 300 people. The real numbers are impressive enough.

title: The Abolitionists
objective: After this level you can explain how Frederick Douglass, William Lloyd Garrison and others argued to end slavery, and why many Northerners opposed them.
summary: Garrison’s Liberator (1831) demanded immediate emancipation; Douglass’s Narrative (1845) answered doubters. Many Northerners objected, and a mob killed Elijah Lovejoy.

cards.headline: Ending slavery was not a popular cause, even in the North.
cards.body: The abolitionists had printing presses, newspapers and one extraordinary witness. They also had enemies in Northern towns. Why?

cards.headline: "I will be heard"
cards.body: On January 1, 1831, William Lloyd Garrison published the first issue of The Liberator. He demanded immediate emancipation, not a slow phase-out, and promised in capital letters: "I WILL BE HEARD." In 1833 he helped organize the American Anti-Slavery Society.

cards.headline: A witness who had lived it
cards.body: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 disguised as a sailor. Some people doubted he had ever been enslaved. So in 1845 he published his Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, partly to answer those doubters. In 1847 he launched his own newspaper, The North Star, despite objections from Garrison and others.

cards.headline: Why many Northerners objected
cards.body: Many Northerners distrusted abolitionists, fearing they threatened harmony between North and South. Critics argued the Constitution left slavery to each state. Demanding immediate emancipation was unpopular even among many Northerners who disliked slavery. Mobs destroyed Elijah Lovejoy’s antislavery press several times, and on November 7, 1837, a mob in Alton, Illinois, killed him as he defended it.

title: Seneca Falls, 1848
objective: After this level you can explain what the Declaration of Sentiments demanded and how the women's rights movement grew alongside abolition.
summary: Shut out in London in 1840, Mott and Stanton organized Seneca Falls in 1848. Their Declaration added women to 1776’s words; the vote was the one split demand.

cards.headline: A women’s movement born at an antislavery meeting that shut women out.
cards.body: Two women were told to sit on the sidelines in London. Eight years later they wrote their own declaration.

mascot.line: It connects: women learned to organize fighting slavery, then turned those skills to their own rights.

cards.headline: Shut out in London
cards.body: At the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, women delegates were refused seats. Among them were Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Walking back together, the two agreed to hold a women’s rights convention of their own. It met at Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19 and 20, 1848.

cards.headline: Two words added
cards.body: Stanton modeled the Declaration of Sentiments on the Declaration of Independence, with a pointed edit: "all men and women are created equal." Then came the grievances. A married woman was, in the eye of the law, "civilly dead," with no right even to the wages she earned.

cards.headline: The boldest demand
cards.body: One resolution demanded women’s right to the elective franchise: the vote. It was the only resolution that did not pass unanimously. Frederick Douglass spoke in support of women’s rights. In the end, 100 people signed the Declaration of Sentiments: 68 women and 32 men.

title: Manifest Destiny
objective: After this level you can explain how Texas, Oregon and the Mexican War added the West, and what that meant for the Mexicans and Native peoples already living there.
summary: Manifest Destiny claimed a right to the continent. Texas joined in 1845, Oregon was split in 1846, and Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its land. Many Mexicans lost theirs.

cards.headline: In a few years the US grew to the Pacific. People already lived there.
cards.body: Texas, Oregon and a war with Mexico remade the map in just a few years. What did the idea behind it promise, and what did it cost?

cards.headline: An idea with a name
cards.body: In 1845 the editor John L. O’Sullivan wrote of "our manifest destiny to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent." Believers held that spreading to the Pacific was the nation’s God-given right. Whigs attacked the idea as warlike and arrogant. For Native nations, as Level 41 showed, expansion had already meant removal.

cards.headline: Texas and Oregon
cards.body: Texas won independence from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States on December 29, 1845. Mexico disputed the border: Texans claimed land to the Rio Grande, Mexico said the Nueces River. In the Northwest, settlers came on the Oregon Trail, and an 1846 treaty with Britain split the Oregon Country along the 49th parallel.

cards.headline: War, and a question from Lincoln
cards.body: President James K. Polk sent troops into the disputed land, and after clashes there Congress declared war on May 13, 1846. Not everyone was convinced. In 1847 Congressman Abraham Lincoln challenged Polk to show whether the spot where the first blood fell was really US soil. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the war: Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its territory, including California, for $15 million.

cards.headline: A promise on paper
cards.body: The treaty let Mexicans in the ceded lands stay and keep their property. But an 1851 law made Mexican landowners in California prove their titles, a slow, costly process. The cost of proving you owned your land was often the land itself.

title: Compromises That Failed
objective: After this level you can explain how the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas-Nebraska Act each tried to settle slavery in the West.
summary: 1820 drew a line at 36°30′. 1850’s Fugitive Slave Act angered the North. The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) erased the line and brought Bleeding Kansas.

cards.headline: Three deals tried to settle slavery in the West. Each one failed.
cards.body: Every time the country gained land, Congress had to answer the same question: slave or free? Watch how each answer came apart.

cards.headline: 1820: draw a line
cards.body: When Missouri asked to join as a slave state, it threatened the balance between slave and free states. The Missouri Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It also banned slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of the Louisiana Territory. A line on a map kept the peace for a generation.

cards.headline: 1850: a package deal
cards.body: The land won from Mexico reopened the question. Senator Henry Clay proposed a package, and Senator Stephen A. Douglas steered it through Congress. California joined as a free state, New Mexico and Utah territories could decide on slavery themselves, and the slave trade ended in Washington, DC.

cards.headline: The part that backfired
cards.body: The price of the deal was a harsher Fugitive Slave Act. It required officials even in free states to arrest suspected freedom seekers, and it punished anyone who helped them escape. It angered many in the North, turning moderate antislavery Northerners into firm opponents of slavery’s spread.

mascot.line: Keep this: each deal settled the last fight over new land, until the next piece of land reopened it.

cards.headline: 1854: erase the line
cards.body: Douglas’s Kansas-Nebraska Act let settlers in those territories decide slavery by popular sovereignty. That repealed the Missouri Compromise line, which had kept slavery out of both. Proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas, and the fighting earned it the name Bleeding Kansas.

objective: After this level you can connect colonial slavery, the founders' compromises and westward expansion to explain why the nation split by 1860.
summary: Lincoln’s 1858 House Divided speech names where the first half of the story led: a nation half slave and half free. Tobacco, slave laws, compromises, cotton and new land all fed the split.

cards.headline: A house divided

Cotton had made slavery more profitable, and each new territory reopened the question the compromises had tried to settle.

title: Dred Scott to Secession
objective: After this level you can explain how the Dred Scott decision, John Brown's raid and Lincoln's election led Southern states to secede.
summary: The Dred Scott ruling, John Brown’s raid and Lincoln’s election came in quick succession. Seven Deep South states seceded, and their own declarations named slavery as the reason.

cards.headline: A court case, a raid and an election broke the Union apart.
cards.body: Americans had argued for decades over slavery in the West. Then three shocks landed within a few years, and each one pushed Southern leaders closer to leaving. Why did they finally go?

cards.headline: The Court slams a door
cards.body: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, sued for his freedom because he had lived in a free state and a free territory. On March 6, 1857, Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled against him and went much further. Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not US citizens, Taney wrote, so Scott could not even sue in federal court. And Congress had no power to ban slavery in the western territories. One ruling shut Scott out of court and threw the West open to slavery.

cards.headline: A raid at Harpers Ferry
cards.body: In October 1859, the abolitionist John Brown led a party of 22 raiders to seize the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to spark a revolt of enslaved people. US Marines under Robert E. Lee captured him, and Virginia hanged him for treason on December 2, 1859. Many Northerners hailed Brown as a martyr. Many white Southerners saw his raid as proof of a Northern plot against the South. The same man looked like a hero or a terrorist, depending on where you stood.

cards.headline: Lincoln wins, the Deep South leaves
cards.body: In November 1860, Republican Abraham Lincoln won the presidency without carrying a single slave state. He opposed slavery’s spread into the western territories, and said he had no purpose to interfere with it where it already existed. For many Southern leaders, that was not enough. South Carolina seceded on December 20, 1860. In February 1861, the seceded Deep South states formed the Confederate States of America, with Jefferson Davis as president; it was seven strong once Texas joined in March.

mascot.line: Keep this one: the seceding states named slavery as their reason, in their own documents.

cards.headline: In their own words
cards.body: Why leave? The seceding states explained it themselves. Several issued declarations of causes that named the defense of slavery as their reason. Mississippi’s was blunt: “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” On this point the evidence is settled, and it comes straight from the people who made the decision.

title: Fort Sumter and the Border States
objective: After this level you can explain how the war began in 1861 and why the border states mattered so much to both sides.
summary: Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861. Lincoln’s call for troops pushed four more states out, while four slave states stayed loyal and shaped his choices.

cards.headline: The first battle of the Civil War killed no one.
cards.body: The shooting started in a harbor. What came next forced every state in between to pick a side, and a few slave states that never left may have decided the war.

cards.headline: Shots at Fort Sumter
cards.body: Fort Sumter was a US fort in Charleston Harbor, inside South Carolina, the first state to secede. On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns opened fire. Major Robert Anderson’s garrison, outnumbered and low on supplies, surrendered. No one was killed in the bombardment itself. But the Civil War, which would last until 1865, had begun.

cards.headline: Lincoln calls, four more states go
cards.body: On April 15, 1861, Lincoln called for 75,000 militia to put down the rebellion. For the states of the Upper South, staying neutral was no longer an option. Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee seceded, bringing the Confederacy to 11 states. A call for troops did what an election alone had not.

cards.headline: The states in between
cards.body: Four slave states never left: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri. These border states held large populations, farms and minerals, and key transportation routes. Losing them would have badly weakened the Union. Lincoln put it plainly in September 1861: “I think to lose Kentucky is nearly the same as to lose the whole game.”

cards.headline: Why it shaped Lincoln’s choices
cards.body: Holding the border states came at a price. Because they still allowed slavery, fear of pushing them toward the Confederacy made Lincoln cautious about freeing enslaved people early in the war. The war’s first goal, for him, was keeping the Union whole.

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
objective: After this level you can explain what the 1863 Proclamation did and did not do, and why Lincoln issued it as a war measure.
summary: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation as a war measure. From January 1, 1863, it freed enslaved people in rebelling areas, spared loyal ones, and opened the Army to Black men.

cards.headline: Lincoln’s most famous order skipped every slave state loyal to the Union.
cards.body: The Emancipation Proclamation declared people free only where the rebellion ruled. Why write it that way, and what did it still change?

cards.headline: Save the Union first
cards.body: In August 1862, Horace Greeley, a New York editor, pressed Lincoln to free the enslaved. Lincoln answered in public: “My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union.” What he didn’t say was that a draft of an emancipation proclamation was already on his desk. The public letter told only half the story.

cards.headline: A war measure
cards.body: The moment came after the Union victory at Antietam. On September 22, 1862, Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation, and the final one took effect on January 1, 1863. He acted as commander in chief, calling it “a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion.” Framed that way, freedom became a weapon against the Confederacy.

cards.headline: What it did, and didn’t
cards.body: It declared that enslaved people in areas in rebellion “are, and henceforward shall be free.” It left slavery untouched in the loyal border states and in Confederate areas the Union already held. But every advance of Union troops after that day widened the area of freedom. And it announced that Black men would be accepted into the Union Army and Navy. Freedom now marched with the army.

title: Black Soldiers, Self-Emancipation
objective: After this level you can explain how Black soldiers and enslaved people escaping to Union lines helped turn the war into a war against slavery.
summary: Enslaved people fleeing to Fort Monroe forced the Union to decide their fate. About 179,000 Black men then served in the Army, and historians still weigh how freedom was won.

cards.headline: Three men in a small boat changed Union policy.
cards.body: Freedom didn’t only come down from Washington. Enslaved people carried the question to the Union Army themselves, and then many put on its uniform.

cards.headline: Contraband of war
cards.body: In May 1861, Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory and James Townsend escaped slavery and rowed to Fort Monroe, a Union fort in Virginia. General Benjamin Butler refused to send them back, declaring people who fled to Union lines “contraband of war.” Within months, hundreds more had come. Three men with a boat had forced the Army to answer a question about freedom.

cards.headline: Liberators in uniform
cards.body: Once the Emancipation Proclamation opened the ranks, about 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army, 10 percent of it, and about 19,000 more served in the Navy. They were first paid $10 a month minus $3 for clothing, while white privates got $13. Congress granted equal pay only in June 1864.

cards.headline: Fort Wagner and the Combahee
cards.body: On June 2, 1863, Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union raid up the Combahee River in South Carolina that freed more than 700 enslaved people. That July, the 54th Massachusetts led an assault on Fort Wagner, also in South Carolina. About 272 of its roughly 650 men were killed, wounded or captured.

mascot.line: Hold both halves: people freed themselves, and the government’s choices mattered too.

cards.headline: Who freed the slaves?
cards.body: Historians have argued about this. Ira Berlin said enslaved people were the prime movers of their own emancipation. James McPherson said Lincoln’s role was decisive. Much recent scholarship shows the pieces working together: people escaping, soldiers fighting, the Proclamation, and laws passed by Congress.

title: Gettysburg
objective: After this level you can explain why the Battle of Gettysburg was a turning point and what Lincoln's address there said the war was for.
summary: Gettysburg ended Lee’s invasion of the North, and Vicksburg fell the next day. At the battlefield cemetery, Lincoln tied the war to 1776 and a new birth of freedom.

cards.headline: The war’s bloodiest battle is best remembered for about 270 words.
cards.body: Three days of fighting turned the war. A few months later, a very short speech explained what all that fighting was for.

cards.headline: Three days in Pennsylvania
cards.body: In the summer of 1863, Robert E. Lee invaded the North for the second time. From July 1 to 3, 1863, his army fought the Union army at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. As many as 51,000 soldiers from both armies were killed, wounded, captured or missing. It was the bloodiest battle of the war.

cards.headline: Pickett’s Charge, then Vicksburg
cards.body: On July 3, 1863, some 12,500 to 15,000 Confederates marched across open fields at the Union center in Pickett’s Charge. The assault failed, and Lee retreated to Virginia, his invasion over. The next day, far to the west, Vicksburg surrendered, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy. In two days, the South lost its invasion and its river.

cards.headline: A few appropriate remarks
cards.body: On November 19, 1863, Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers killed at Gettysburg. “Four score and seven years ago” counted back 87 years to 1776, and to the proposition “that all men are created equal.” He closed by resolving that the nation “shall have a new birth of freedom,” and that government “of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.”

title: Total War and the Home Fronts
objective: After this level you can explain how Sherman's march, the draft and women's war work brought the war to civilians in North and South.
summary: Sherman marched through Georgia to wreck the South’s ability to fight. At home, drafts that let the rich buy out sparked riots, and women ran hospitals and protested hunger.

cards.headline: Late in the war, the fighting spread far beyond the battlefields.
cards.body: It reached city streets, kitchens and hospital wards, and the farms in the path of an army marching across Georgia.

cards.headline: Marching through Georgia
cards.body: Union general William T. Sherman captured Atlanta on September 2, 1864, a victory that helped Lincoln win reelection that November. From November 15 to December 21, 1864, Sherman’s army marched about 285 miles to Savannah, living off the land and destroying railroads and supplies. His aim was to wreck the Confederacy’s ability to make war and bring the war home to Southern civilians.

cards.headline: A rich man’s war?
cards.body: Both sides turned to drafting soldiers. The Confederacy passed the first national draft in American history in April 1862. The Union’s Enrollment Act of March 3, 1863, let a drafted man hire a substitute or pay $300 to stay home. Critics called it “a rich man’s war but a poor man’s fight.”

cards.headline: Anger at home
cards.body: In July 1863, New York City draft rioters turned on Black residents and burned the Colored Orphan Asylum. More than 100 people were killed. In the South, hunger boiled over. On April 2, 1863, women in Richmond, the Confederate capital, many of them soldiers’ wives, rioted over food prices, crying “Bread or blood!”

cards.headline: Women’s war work
cards.body: Women took on new public roles. Dorothea Dix became superintendent of women nurses for the Union Army in 1861, and thousands of women served as nurses.

summary: Lincoln called for peace “with malice toward none.” Lee surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, 1865. Days later Lincoln was killed, and Andrew Johnson’s lenient terms set off a fight with Congress.

cards.headline: The war ended in a quiet Virginia village. Within a week, Lincoln was dead.
cards.body: That April brought the Union its victory and its greatest loss. Who would now decide how the South rejoined the nation?

cards.headline: With malice toward none
cards.body: On March 4, 1865, with victory near, Lincoln gave his second inaugural address. He said slavery was “somehow the cause of the war.” And he urged the nation on “with malice toward none, with charity for all.” It was a call for peace without revenge.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize both totals. Remember that new evidence can move even a famous number.

cards.headline: Surrender at Appomattox
cards.body: Robert E. Lee surrendered his army to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865. Grant’s terms let Confederate soldiers go home on parole, and those who owned horses or mules could keep them for farming. The cost of the war was staggering: about 620,000 soldiers died by the long-accepted count, and a 2011 census-based study by J. David Hacker estimated about 750,000.

cards.headline: A shot at Ford’s Theatre
cards.body: On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, shot Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington. Lincoln died the next morning, and Andrew Johnson, a Southerner who had opposed secession, became president. Johnson pardoned most white Southerners and let former Confederate states rebuild their governments with little federal oversight. Many Republicans in Congress were outraged. The peace would now be fought over in Washington.

title: Three Amendments
objective: After this level you can explain what the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments promised and why they are called the second founding.
summary: The 13th Amendment ended slavery, the 14th made everyone born here a citizen with equal protection, and the 15th barred race in voting. Eric Foner calls them a second founding.

cards.headline: Three amendments rewrote who counted as an American.
cards.body: After the war, Congress and the states changed the Constitution itself. Freedom came first, then citizenship, then the vote.

cards.headline: The 13th: freedom
cards.body: The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, abolished slavery in the United States. It kept one exception: slavery and involuntary servitude were banned “except as a punishment for crime.” Six words, easy to miss.

cards.headline: The 14th: citizens and equals
cards.body: The 14th Amendment, ratified July 9, 1868, made “all persons born or naturalized in the United States” citizens. Congress wrote that clause to undo the Dred Scott decision. The amendment also barred states from denying any person “due process of law” or “the equal protection of the laws.”

cards.headline: The 15th: the vote
cards.body: The 15th Amendment, ratified February 3, 1870, barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It said nothing about sex. That split the women’s rights movement: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed the amendment for leaving women out, while Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass supported it as a step that could pass.

cards.headline: A second founding
cards.body: Historian Eric Foner calls these three amendments a “second founding” because they remade the Constitution. Freedom, birthright citizenship, equal protection and a vote without racial bars were now part of the nation’s founding law.

title: Reconstruction Rises and Falls
objective: After this level you can explain what Reconstruction achieved, the violence that opposed it, and the bargain of 1877 that ended it.
summary: Freedpeople built schools and elected Black lawmakers to Congress. Klan terror and massacres fought back, and after the disputed 1876 election federal troops left the South in 1877.

cards.headline: Freedpeople built schools and won elections. Why did Reconstruction end so soon?
cards.body: For about a decade, the South was remade. Then violence and a political bargain undid much of it.

cards.headline: Building freedom
cards.body: Congress created the Freedmen’s Bureau on March 3, 1865. It set up schools, oversaw labor contracts between freedpeople and employers, and helped families separated by slavery find each other again.

cards.headline: Black lawmakers
cards.body: With the 15th Amendment barring race discrimination in voting, Black men voted and won office. In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American US senator. On December 12, 1870, Joseph Rainey of South Carolina, born enslaved, became the first African American in the House.

cards.headline: Terror
cards.body: Confederate veterans founded the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865 or 1866, and it used terror against Black Americans to undo Reconstruction. On April 13, 1873, armed white men attacked Black defenders of the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana. Estimates of the Black dead run as high as about 150.

mascot.line: Keep the order: rights written into law, then undone by violence and politics.

cards.headline: The bargain of 1877
cards.body: The 1876 presidential election was disputed. Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president, and in 1877 he withdrew the last federal troops protecting Southern Republican governments. Historian C. Vann Woodward (1951) argued a secret bargain settled the election. Allan Peskin (1973) questioned whether it was a true compromise. Either way, federal protection was gone.

cards.headline: Won, then lost

The gains were real: Freedmen’s Bureau schools, and Black lawmakers like Hiram Revels in Congress. So was the backlash, from Klan terror to the bargain of 1877. The war settled slavery for good. Reconstruction’s promises stayed in the Constitution, waiting for later generations to enforce them.

title: Rails, Homesteads and Bison
objective: After this level you can explain how the transcontinental railroad and the Homestead Act opened the Plains, and how the bison were nearly wiped out.
summary: In 1869 two railroads met at Promontory Summit, and the Homestead Act drew settlers west. Railways, hide hunters and the army cut the bison from tens of millions to under 1,000.

cards.headline: Trains crossed the continent in 1869. By the 1890s the bison were nearly gone.
cards.body: The same years that tied the country together with iron almost wiped out the animal the Plains nations lived on. Here’s how rails, farms and hunters remade the Plains.

cards.headline: Two railroads race to meet
cards.body: In 1862 Congress passed the first Pacific Railroad Act. The Union Pacific built west from Nebraska, the Central Pacific built east from California, and the two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. By the end, Chinese immigrants made up about 90 percent of the Central Pacific’s workforce. The country’s new steel spine was built largely by immigrant hands.
cards.callout: The rails met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869

cards.headline: Free land, with conditions
cards.body: In 1862 Lincoln also signed the Homestead Act. It offered 160 acres of public land for a filing fee, as long as you lived on it and farmed it. The people who tried to “prove up” came from all walks of life: immigrants, farmers without land of their own, single women and formerly enslaved people. A farm of your own, for the price of hard work and paperwork.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 7’s horses made Plains peoples expert bison hunters. Lose the bison, and that whole way of life is under attack.

cards.headline: The Great Slaughter
cards.body: Bison once numbered an estimated 30 to 60 million. Railways, rifles and an international market for hides drove the “Great Slaughter,” from about 1820 to 1880. The US military also encouraged destroying the herds, as a way to control the Native nations who depended on them. By the 1890s, fewer than 1,000 bison were left. A whole way of life was losing its foundation.

title: Wars for the West
objective: After this level you can explain the wars between the US Army and the Plains nations, from Little Bighorn in 1876 to Wounded Knee in 1890.
summary: The US recognized the Black Hills as Sioux land in 1868, then gold brought miners and war. The Lakota and allies beat Custer in 1876; at Wounded Knee in 1890 soldiers killed about 150 to 300 Lakota.

cards.headline: In 1876 the Lakota beat Custer at the Little Bighorn. In 1890 came Wounded Knee.
cards.body: Between those dates, the Plains nations fought to keep their homelands. The story starts with a promise about some hills.

cards.headline: A promise, then gold
cards.body: In the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, the United States recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation. Then, in 1874, George Armstrong Custer led an expedition into the Black Hills. Gold was found, and miners poured in. The government ordered the Lakota back to reservations by January 31, 1876, or be treated as hostile. A treaty is a promise on paper. Gold turned out to be heavier.

cards.headline: The Little Bighorn
cards.body: The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne were Plains nations. On June 25, 1876, at the Little Bighorn, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer. He and every soldier who followed him into the battle were killed. The victory was stunning, and short: the army flooded the region and forced the bands to surrender.

cards.headline: Wounded Knee
cards.body: By 1890 the Lakota faced hunger and a shrinking reservation, and some turned to the Ghost Dance, a religion that alarmed some US officials. On December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee Creek, the 7th Cavalry killed about 150 to 300 Lakota, almost half of them women and children.
cards.callout: Estimates of the dead at Wounded Knee range from about 150 to 300

cards.headline: The claim that stayed
cards.body: The Lakota never dropped their claim to the Black Hills. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled that the land had been taken and payment was owed. The Sioux refused the money. They wanted the land.

title: Boarding Schools and Allotment
objective: After this level you can explain how boarding schools and the Dawes Act aimed to erase Native cultures and cost Native nations most of their remaining land.
summary: Boarding schools like Carlisle (1879) tried to strip Native children of their languages. The Dawes Act (1887) cut Native land from about 138 to 48 million acres.

cards.headline: After the wars came a quieter campaign: classrooms and surveyors.
cards.body: Its backers expected that farms and schooling would make Native people drop their own cultures. Here’s how it worked, and how Native people answered.

cards.headline: “Kill the Indian, save the man”
cards.body: In 1879, army officer Richard Henry Pratt opened a boarding school for Native children in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. He described his aim as to “kill the Indian in him, and save the man.” Boarding schools separated children from their families, cut their hair, changed their names and dress, and forbade their own languages. The target wasn’t the child. It was everything the child had learned at home.

cards.headline: Writing back
cards.body: Zitkála-Šá, a Yankton Dakota girl, was sent to a boarding school at 8. As an adult writer, she exposed its harms in essays in The Atlantic Monthly in 1900. In 1926 she and her husband founded the National Council of American Indians. The schools tried to take her voice. She used their English to be heard across the country.

cards.headline: Cutting up the land
cards.body: The Dawes Act of 1887 split reservation land, held in common, into individual allotments: a quarter section, 160 acres, for each head of family. Whatever was left over was declared “surplus” and could be sold to non-Native settlers. Picture a shared family farm divided into lots, with the leftover lots sold to strangers.

cards.headline: What the numbers show
cards.body: Native nations held about 138 million acres before the Dawes Act and only about 48 million by 1934, when the Indian Reorganization Act ended allotment. That’s nearly two-thirds of their land gone, without a single battle.
cards.callout: About 138 million acres before the Dawes Act; about 48 million by 1934

title: Gilded Age Giants
objective: After this level you can explain how Carnegie and Rockefeller built giant companies, and why Americans called such men both robber barons and captains of industry.
summary: The Gilded Age is named for an 1873 novel. Carnegie rose from bobbin boy to steel king; Standard Oil came to refine 90 to 95 percent of US oil. Historians still split over robber barons or builders.

cards.headline: Americans called the same men robber barons and captains of industry.
cards.body: Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller built giant companies. How they did it explains why people still argue about them.

cards.headline: Gold on the outside
cards.body: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner gave the era its name in their 1873 novel The Gilded Age. Gilded means thinly covered in gold: dazzling on the surface, and who knows underneath. Keep that picture handy as you meet two of the era’s giants.

cards.headline: From bobbin boy to steel
cards.body: Andrew Carnegie’s family came from Scotland to Pittsburgh in 1848, and at 13 he worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill. He went on to build a steel empire, and in 1901 sold his company to J.P. Morgan for $480 million. In 1889 he had argued that the rich have a duty to use their surplus wealth for the improvement of mankind: the Gospel of Wealth.

cards.headline: One company, almost all the oil
cards.body: John D. Rockefeller’s Standard Oil Company was incorporated in Ohio in 1870. By 1880, by buying out rivals, merging with other firms and using railroad rebates, it refined 90 to 95 percent of US oil. That’s nine or more of every ten barrels refined in the country, passing through one company.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: “robber baron” and “captain of industry” aren’t two groups of men. They’re two verdicts on the same men.

cards.headline: Robber barons or builders?
cards.body: Historians read the same record in opposite ways. In his 1934 book The Robber Barons, Matthew Josephson cast these men as unscrupulous pirates grabbing the economy. In a 1940 biography, Allan Nevins argued that Rockefeller, despite unethical tactics, brought order to a chaotic industry. Both sides look at the same rebates, refineries and fortunes.

title: Workers Organize
objective: After this level you can explain why industrial workers struck and formed unions, and what the Triangle fire of 1911 changed.
summary: Workers formed unions to bargain as a group. Homestead (1892) was a defeat, the 1909 shirtwaist strike won gains, and the 1911 Triangle fire led to new safety laws.

cards.headline: In 1911, 146 garment workers died in a fire. Many exits were locked.
cards.body: Why did workers keep organizing and striking in these decades, and what finally changed the rules?

cards.headline: Bargaining as a group
cards.body: A labor union is an association of workers that seeks better pay and conditions by bargaining with employers as a group. Employers didn’t always accept that. In 1892, at Carnegie’s Homestead steel works in Pennsylvania, managers locked out the workers and sent 300 Pinkerton agents to seize the plant. The battle left three Pinkertons and seven strikers dead, and the state militia broke the strike and the union.

cards.headline: The Uprising of the 20,000
cards.body: In November 1909, Clara Lemlich, 23, stood up at a New York meeting and called for a general strike. Thousands of shirtwaist makers, mostly young immigrant women, walked out. The strike lasted over two months and won better pay and shorter hours at many shops. The people sewing the country’s blouses had shown they could shut the shops down.

cards.headline: Locked doors
cards.body: On March 25, 1911, fire broke out at the Triangle Waist Company in New York. The doors were locked or opened inward, and many exits were blocked or broken. 146 garment workers died, mostly young immigrant women.
cards.callout: 146 workers died in the Triangle fire of March 25, 1911

cards.headline: What changed
cards.body: New York set up a Factory Investigating Commission, which led to more than 30 health and safety laws, including fire codes and limits on child labor. One witness to the fire, Frances Perkins, later became US Secretary of Labor. The fire made the case the strikers had been making.

cards.body: Between 1880 and 1920, a great wave of immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe. Between 1881 and 1924, over 2.5 million eastern European Jews alone arrived, driven by persecution and poverty.

cards.headline: Ellis Island
cards.body: Ellis Island opened in New York Harbor in 1892, and more than 12 million immigrants passed through it by 1924. Only about 2 percent were refused entry, most often for contagious disease.

cards.headline: A door shut by law
cards.body: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers. It was the first major US law to suspend immigration by a single nationality. It stood until 1943, when Congress repealed the exclusion laws while China was a World War II ally.

cards.headline: Angel Island
cards.body: Angel Island Immigration Station opened in San Francisco Bay in 1910, the main western entry point for immigrants from Asia. Chinese and Japanese immigrants were often held there for weeks or months while officials checked their papers. Chinese detainees carved poems into the barracks walls, expressing frustration and sorrow.

title: Jim Crow
objective: After this level you can explain how segregation laws, Plessy v. Ferguson and voting barriers undid Reconstruction's gains, and how Ida B. Wells fought back.
summary: Homer Plessy’s planned 1892 challenge led to Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which allowed segregation. Poll taxes and literacy tests shut out Black voters, and Ida B. Wells exposed lynching.

cards.headline: In 1892, a New Orleans man sat in the “wrong” train car on purpose.
cards.body: Homer Plessy was testing a law. His case would decide whether states could segregate Americans by race.

cards.headline: A planned challenge
cards.body: Louisiana’s Separate Car Act of 1890 required separate railway cars for Black and white passengers. A New Orleans civil rights group, the Comité des Citoyens, recruited Homer Plessy to test it. In 1892 he sat in a whites-only car. The arrest was the plan, not the problem.

mascot.line: Keep this: the 13th Amendment ended slavery, but Plessy let states write inequality into law.

cards.headline: “Separate but equal”
cards.body: In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 1 that segregation was constitutional if facilities were “equal.” The lone dissenter, Justice John Marshall Harlan, wrote: “Our Constitution is color-blind.” The majority’s rule became the legal backbone of Jim Crow.

cards.headline: Closing the ballot box
cards.body: From Mississippi in 1890 to Georgia in 1908, every former Confederate state moved to disfranchise Black voters. Their tools were poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses, which kept Black men from voting without saying “race” in the law.

cards.headline: Ida B. Wells fights back
cards.body: In 1892 a Memphis mob lynched Ida B. Wells’s friend Thomas Moss and two other Black grocers who competed with a white-owned store. Wells investigated lynchings and found the usual excuse for them was almost always false. A mob destroyed her newspaper’s office; she published anyway, in the pamphlet Southern Horrors. In 1909 she took part in founding the NAACP.

title: The Progressives

summary: Ida Tarbell exposed Standard Oil, broken up in 1911. The Jungle (1906) led to the Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts. Nast’s cartoons helped topple Boss Tweed; Jane Addams founded Hull-House.

cards.headline: A novel about a Chicago meatpacking plant made Congress act.
cards.body: The Progressives believed that if people saw what was happening, they would demand change. Reporters, cartoonists and reformers set out to show them.

cards.headline: The reporter and the monopoly
cards.body: Remember Standard Oil? Ida Tarbell’s History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), first serialized in McClure’s magazine, exposed its unfair tactics and railroad rebates. In 1911 the Supreme Court ruled that Standard Oil had broken the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered it split into 34 companies. From book to breakup took just seven years.

cards.headline: The Jungle
cards.body: Upton Sinclair’s novel The Jungle (1906) exposed filthy, dangerous conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking plants. Readers were disgusted, and public outrage helped pass the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act, both in 1906.
cards.callout: The Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act both passed in 1906

cards.headline: Cleaning up the cities
cards.body: Boss William Tweed’s Tammany Hall ring plundered New York City of an estimated $30 million to $200 million. Thomas Nast’s cartoons helped expose it, and Tweed was convicted in 1873. Reformers also built. In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House in Chicago, offering immigrant neighbors classes, childcare and job help.

title: Votes for Women
objective: After this level you can explain how suffragists won the vote state by state in the West and then nationally with the 19th Amendment in 1920.
summary: Wyoming women voted from 1869, and the West led. Catt’s lobbying and Paul’s pickets won the 19th Amendment in 1920. Many Black and Native women were still shut out.

cards.headline: Women in Wyoming were voting half a century before the 19th Amendment.
cards.body: The fight for the vote was won in pieces: first out West, then in Washington, then in one tense vote in Tennessee.

cards.headline: The West goes first
cards.body: On December 10, 1869, Wyoming Territory became the first place in the United States to grant women the vote. Women of the West went on to be the first in the country to win full voting rights, state by state and territory by territory. By the time the national fight peaked, the map already had a head start on one side.

cards.headline: Two strategies
cards.body: In 1916 Carrie Chapman Catt’s “Winning Plan” paired promising state campaigns with lobbying for a federal amendment. Alice Paul took a louder road. From January 1917 her “Silent Sentinels” picketed the White House, and many were arrested. Sentenced to seven months in jail, Paul led a hunger strike. One side persuaded; the other refused to be ignored.

cards.headline: Tennessee decides
cards.body: On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, after a young legislator, Harry Burn, cast the deciding vote. Burn said he changed his vote after a letter from his mother urging him to support suffrage. Never underestimate a letter from home.
cards.callout: Tennessee ratified the 19th Amendment on August 18, 1920

cards.headline: Who still couldn’t vote
cards.body: The amendment didn’t reach everyone. In the South, Black women who tried to register faced poll taxes, literacy tests and violence, the same barriers from Level 67. Many Native American women could not vote either, because they were not recognized as citizens until 1924.

title: 1898 and an Overseas Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how the war with Spain in 1898 gave the US overseas colonies, and what imperialists and anti-imperialists argued.
summary: A war to free Cuba in 1898 ended with the US holding Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines and Hawaii, and with Americans arguing over empire.

cards.headline: In 1898 the US went to war to free Cuba. It came home with an empire.
cards.body: Spain handed over islands in two oceans. How did a war over someone else's independence end with American colonies, and who objected?

cards.headline: Remember the Maine
cards.body: Cuban revolutionaries had fought Spain since 1895, and many Americans cheered them on. On February 15, 1898, the US battleship Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor. On April 25, 1898, the US declared war on Spain, and in the Teller Amendment Congress promised not to annex Cuba. Notice the fine print: that promise covered one island only.

cards.headline: Islands in two oceans
cards.body: In the Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, Spain ceded Puerto Rico and Guam and sold the Philippines to the US for $20 million. That same year the US annexed Hawaii, where planters and businessmen backed by US Marines had overthrown Queen Liliuokalani in 1893. Hawaiians had pushed back: in 1897 more than 21,000 Native Hawaiians signed petitions against annexation.

cards.headline: The Filipinos' own war
cards.body: Filipinos had revolted against Spain too. Led by Emilio Aguinaldo, they proclaimed an independent Philippine Republic. They wanted independence, not new rulers, and fought the Philippine-American War from 1899 to 1902. By the State Department historians' count, over 4,200 US and over 20,000 Filipino soldiers died, and as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians.

mascot.line: This connects: the anti-imperialists turned the Declaration from Level 25 into an argument against ruling other peoples.

cards.headline: Empire or liberty?
cards.body: Backers of annexation wanted Asian trade, doubted Filipinos could govern themselves, and feared Germany or Japan would take the islands. The Anti-Imperialist League, which included Andrew Carnegie, Mark Twain and Samuel Gompers, answered with the Declaration of Independence: governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed."

title: World War I
objective: After this level you can explain why the US stayed out of World War I until 1917, what each side of the argument over joining said, and what American troops changed.
summary: Submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram took the US to war in 1917 over strong objections; American troops, Black and Native soldiers among them, fought in France.

cards.headline: Wilson was reelected in 1916 for keeping out of war. In 1917 he asked for one.
cards.body: What changed in a few months, who said no, and what did American soldiers do once they got to France?

cards.headline: Neutral, then not
cards.body: When war broke out in Europe in 1914, Wilson declared the US neutral. A German submarine sank the liner Lusitania on May 7, 1915, killing 128 Americans, yet he kept the country out. Then, on February 1, 1917, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare. The Zimmermann Telegram invited Mexico to join Germany and "reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona."

cards.headline: Yes and no in Congress
cards.body: On April 2, 1917, Wilson asked Congress for war: "The world must be made safe for democracy." Opponents in the House argued no vital interest was threatened, the public didn't want war, and arms makers and business interests were pushing it; American bankers had loaned the Allies over $2 billion. The House voted 373 to 50. Jeannette Rankin, the first woman in Congress, said: "I cannot vote for war." Congress declared war on April 6, 1917.

cards.headline: Late, but in huge numbers
cards.body: Over a million American soldiers fought in the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, the largest US operation of the war. It ran from September 26, 1918, until the armistice of November 11, 1918, when the fighting stopped.

cards.headline: Who fought
cards.body: The 369th Infantry, a Black regiment called the Harlem Hellfighters, spent 191 days in front-line trenches, more than any US unit its size. In France in 1918, Choctaw soldiers became the first Code Talkers, sending battle messages in Choctaw that the enemy never broke.

title: The Great Migration and Harlem
objective: After this level you can explain why millions of Black Southerners moved north and how the Harlem Renaissance grew from it.
summary: About six million Black Southerners moved north and west to escape Jim Crow and find work, and in Harlem writers like Langston Hughes celebrated Black culture.

cards.headline: About six million Black Southerners packed up and moved north and west.
cards.body: It was one of the largest migrations in US history. Why did they go, and what did they build when they got there?

cards.headline: Pushed and pulled
cards.body: From the 1910s to the 1970s, migrants left the South to escape racial violence and the oppression of Jim Crow, and to find better jobs and schooling. World War I opened the door. From 1917, men leaving for the war and a drop in immigration from Europe left factory jobs that Black workers could now fill. Every train ticket north was a vote against Jim Crow.

cards.headline: New cities, old prejudice
cards.body: Migrants built new lives in cities such as New York, Chicago and Detroit. But the North had its own color line. Migrants met discrimination, including in housing, and racial violence in the Red Summer of 1919. Leaving the South didn't mean leaving racism behind.

cards.headline: Harlem's renaissance
cards.body: In New York's Harlem, the newcomers helped spark the Harlem Renaissance, which celebrated African American culture and achievement. Langston Hughes, whose first book of poems, The Weary Blues, appeared in 1926, became one of its leading writers. He said the people he met every day inspired his work, and blues and jazz gave it rhythm.

title: The Roaring Twenties and Prohibition
objective: After this level you can explain what changed in the 1920s, and why Americans banned alcohol in 1920 and repealed the ban in 1933.
summary: In a newly urban nation, temperance reformers won national Prohibition in 1920; bootlegging, crime and the Depression, plus a women's repeal movement, ended it in 1933.

cards.headline: In 1920 the US banned alcohol. In 1933 it changed its mind.
cards.body: Why would a nation amend its Constitution to stop people drinking, then amend it again to undo the ban?

cards.headline: A new kind of country
cards.body: The decade opened on a changed nation. The 1920 census was the first in which most Americans lived in urban areas. That same year, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, completing women's right to vote nationwide. New city crowds and new voters would both shape the fight over drinking.

cards.headline: The dry crusade
cards.body: From the 1870s the Women's Christian Temperance Union saw alcohol as the source of many social ills, including ruined families. Reformers won the 18th Amendment, which banned the "manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors" for drinking. National Prohibition began in January 1920.

cards.headline: Speakeasies and gangsters
cards.body: Illegal liquor stayed easy to find. Gangsters like Al Capone grew rich from bootlegging and bribed police, judges and politicians. The law meant to clean up society had created a booming criminal industry.

cards.headline: Women for repeal
cards.body: In 1929 Pauline Sabin founded the Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform. Its members argued Prohibition had led to more unregulated and underage drinking and to distrust of the law, and it grew to 1.5 million reported members. After the 1929 crash, the promise of jobs and tax revenue added support. The 21st Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the 18th.

title: The Crash and the Dust Bowl
objective: After this level you can describe how ordinary Americans lived through the Great Depression and why the Dust Bowl drove families off the Plains.
summary: After the 1929 crash, a quarter of workers lost their jobs, Hoovervilles spread, Mexican Americans were pushed out, and on the southern Plains drought and dust storms drove families west.

cards.headline: By 1933, about one American worker in four had no job.
cards.body: Economists argue over why the economy collapsed. This level is about how people lived through it, and why some fled a wall of dust.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the percentages. Keep the order: the crash in 1929, the worst joblessness in 1933.

cards.headline: From crash to shantytown
cards.body: On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the stock market fell nearly 12 percent, and by mid-November it had lost almost half its value. In 1933, at the worst, 24.9 percent of workers had no job. Homeless families built shantytowns from packing crates and scrap, nicknamed "Hoovervilles."

cards.headline: Black Sunday
cards.body: On the southern Plains, repeated droughts struck farms that had spread onto poorer land and cut back on soil conservation. The soil started to blow away. On Black Sunday, April 14, 1935, a wall of dust turned a sunny afternoon darker than night. That year an Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, coined a name for the region: the Dust Bowl.

cards.headline: On the road, and out
cards.body: Many Plains families, called "Okies," abandoned their farms and headed to California in search of work. Others were pushed out of the country. Officials pressed Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many of them US-born citizens, to leave for Mexico. Estimates range from 400,000 to 2 million people.

title: The New Deal
objective: After this level you can name the New Deal's main programs, including Social Security in 1935, and explain who they helped and who they left out.
summary: FDR's New Deal put millions to work and created Social Security in 1935, but it left out farm and domestic workers, most Black workers among them, and drew critics from both sides.

cards.headline: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself," FDR told the nation in 1933.
cards.body: Then he launched the New Deal. What did it build, who did it leave out, and who said it went too far or not far enough?

cards.headline: Putting people to work
cards.body: New Deal agencies such as the CCC (1933) and the WPA put unemployed Americans to work on conservation, construction and arts projects. By 1942, over 2.5 million men had served in the CCC. The Social Security Act, signed August 14, 1935, created old-age benefits and unemployment insurance. For Native nations, the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended allotment.

cards.headline: Who was left out
cards.body: Social Security left out agricultural workers and domestic servants in private homes. In 1935 the NAACP's Charles Hamilton Houston warned Congress this would leave out Black sharecroppers and tenants, and about 65 percent of African Americans were left out. Why were they excluded? Social Security historian Larry DeWitt argues the reason was the practical problem of collecting taxes, not racial motives.

cards.headline: Too far, or not far enough?
cards.body: Critics came from both sides. The American Liberty League, founded in 1934 by business leaders and politicians, attacked the New Deal as unconstitutional. Senator Huey Long pushed his Share Our Wealth plan to spread wealth more widely, and by 1935 its societies claimed more than seven million members.

title: The Road to Pearl Harbor
objective: After this level you can explain how the US moved from neutrality to aiding Britain, and why Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.
summary: Still bitter about World War I, Congress passed Neutrality Acts, but FDR moved toward aiding Britain; an embargo on Japan led to the attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.

cards.headline: On December 7, 1941, Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor pulled the US into the war.
cards.body: Yet for years most Americans had wanted no part of another world war. How did the country get from neutral to Pearl Harbor?

cards.headline: Never again
cards.body: In the 1930s, Senator Gerald Nye's report claimed bankers and arms makers had pushed the US into World War I for their own profit. Congress listened. The first Neutrality Act, passed August 31, 1935, banned exporting "arms, ammunition, and implements of war" to nations at war.

cards.headline: Leaning toward Britain
cards.body: In November 1939 a new Neutrality Act let nations at war buy arms on a "cash and carry" basis, which mostly helped Britain. In 1940 FDR won a third term. Under Lend-Lease, passed in March 1941, the US supplied Britain with war materials without demanding immediate payment. Many Americans opposed another war, and Army chief George Marshall argued supplies should be saved to defend the Western Hemisphere.

cards.headline: Oil, embargo, attack
cards.body: As Japan pushed into China and Indochina, the US froze Japanese assets and cut off exports to Japan, including oil. Japan's leaders decided to strike. The attack on Pearl Harbor killed more than 2,400 Americans. The next day the US declared war on Japan, and when Germany declared war on the US, it faced war in Europe and Asia.

Revisionists such as Gar Alperovitz argue they were unnecessary since Japan was near surrender, and partly aimed at the Soviets.

title: The Home Front and Incarceration
objective: After this level you can explain how World War II changed work for women and Black Americans, and why Japanese Americans were forced into camps.
summary: World War II put six million women into war jobs and pushed Black Americans to demand a double victory, while Executive Order 9066 forced about 122,000 Japanese Americans into camps.

cards.headline: In 1942 the government forced about 122,000 Japanese Americans from their homes.
cards.body: The same war opened factory gates to women and Black workers. How could one war widen freedom for some and take it from others?

cards.headline: Rosie and the Double V
cards.body: More than six million women took wartime factory jobs; Rosie the Riveter became their symbol. Labor leader A. Philip Randolph threatened to bring tens of thousands of Black marchers to Washington unless defense jobs opened to them. The result was Executive Order 8802 of June 25, 1941: "There shall be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries." In 1942 the Pittsburgh Courier launched the Double V campaign: victory over fascism abroad and racism at home.

cards.headline: Executive Order 9066
cards.body: Executive Order 9066, issued February 19, 1942, led to the forced removal of about 122,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast. Nearly 70,000 of them were US citizens. None were charged with a crime, and they had no way to appeal. The government called the guarded camps "relocation centers"; they were also known as "internment camps." This level uses the plainer word: incarceration.

cards.headline: Fighting back, and an apology
cards.body: Gordon Hirabayashi and Fred Korematsu challenged the orders in court, but the Supreme Court upheld them. More than 30,000 Japanese Americans served in the war, in segregated units. In 1988 Congress apologized for the incarceration and paid $20,000 to each person who had been held.

title: The Cold War Begins
objective: After this level you can explain containment, the Korean War, the nuclear arms race and the Red Scare at home.
summary: Containment, from the Truman Doctrine to Korea, set US Cold War policy. The Soviet bomb of 1949 started an arms race, and McCarthy’s Red Scare mixed real spying with accusations made on little proof.

cards.body: How did a rivalry with the Soviet Union shape wars abroad and fear at home?

cards.headline: Hold the line
cards.body: In March 1947 President Harry Truman asked Congress for $400 million in aid to Greece and Turkey. It would be US policy, he said, “to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.” That same year diplomat George Kennan called for “patient but firm and vigilant containment” of Soviet expansion. The plan in one word: containment. Don’t attack; block every push.

cards.headline: A hot war and a bigger bomb
cards.body: On June 25, 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea, and United Nations forces fought to defend the South. An armistice on July 27, 1953, stopped the fighting with Korea still divided near the 38th parallel, and no peace treaty. The rivalry also went nuclear. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in August 1949, ending the US monopoly. The US tested the far stronger hydrogen bomb in 1952, and the arms race was on.

mascot.line: Keep this: two things are true at once. Soviet spies were real, and McCarthy’s accusations came with little proof.

cards.headline: Fear at home
cards.body: In Wheeling, West Virginia, on February 9, 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed to have a list of Communists in the State Department. He offered little proof, yet his accusations made him famous until the Senate censured him on December 2, 1954. Soviet spying was real, though. Decoded Soviet cables released in 1995, the Venona project, confirmed that Soviet spies had worked inside the US government.

cards.headline: The Cold War begins: explained
learned: Containment meant blocking Soviet expansion
Korea ended in an armistice in 1953, not a peace
The Soviet bomb of 1949 began the arms race
McCarthy had little proof, but Soviet spying was real

With a peace treaty that reunited Korea

options.rationale: The line stayed near the 38th parallel.

options.label: With a US atomic bomb on North Korea
options.rationale: No bomb was used; an armistice stopped the fighting.

questions.explanation: An armistice on July 27, 1953, stopped the fighting, but no peace treaty was ever signed.

options.label: Leave it alone, since it is far away
options.rationale: Containment meant blocking each push, even far away.

options.label: Invade the Soviet Union to end the threat
options.rationale: Containment blocked expansion; it didn’t attack the Soviet Union.

options.label: Help that country resist, as with Greece and Korea

title: The GI Bill and the Suburbs
objective: After this level you can explain how the GI Bill, federal mortgages and interstate highways built the postwar suburbs, and who was shut out.
summary: The GI Bill of 1944, mass-built towns like Levittown and the interstate highways built the postwar suburbs. Covenants and FHA redlining kept most Black families, veterans included, out.

cards.headline: Levittown: more than 17,000 new houses, and Black families barred.
cards.body: How did the federal government help build the suburbs, and who did it leave outside?

cards.headline: A bill for veterans
cards.body: President Franklin Roosevelt signed the GI Bill on June 22, 1944, days after D-Day. It gave World War II veterans money for college, unemployment pay and help buying homes. Within seven years, about eight million veterans had used its education benefits. A diploma, then a mortgage: that’s how many families climbed.

cards.headline: Houses on an assembly line
cards.body: Builders raced to meet the demand. Between 1947 and 1951, Levitt & Sons mass-produced more than 17,000 houses at Levittown on Long Island, New York. Then the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, signed by President Dwight Eisenhower, funded about 41,000 miles of interstate highways. Cheap houses plus fast roads: that’s the suburban recipe.

cards.headline: Who was shut out
cards.body: Levittown’s early leases and deeds barred occupancy “by any person other than members of the Caucasian race,” and even after that clause was dropped, Levitt refused to sell to Black families. The Federal Housing Administration largely refused to insure mortgages in Black neighborhoods and steered lenders toward segregated ones. So Black veterans, promised the same GI Bill, were often unable to get its home loans and were largely kept out of the new white suburbs.

cards.headline: The GI Bill and the suburbs: explained
learned: The GI Bill (1944) paid for college and home loans
Levittown and the interstates built the suburbs
Covenants and FHA redlining shut Black families out

options.label: A free house in any suburb they chose

options.label: A pension paid only to officers
options.rationale: It covered veterans broadly, not just officers.

options.label: Money for college, unemployment pay and home-buying help

options.label: The GI Bill paid only for college, never homes
options.rationale: The GI Bill did include help buying homes.

options.label: Veterans had to wait ten years to use home loans
options.rationale: No such waiting rule appears in the level.

options.label: Both paid for veterans’ college
options.rationale: The Homestead Act had nothing to do with college.

options.label: Both gave land to railroad companies
options.rationale: Neither is about railroad grants here.

options.label: Both used federal help to put people in homes

questions.explanation: The Homestead Act offered land to settlers; the GI Bill helped veterans buy homes. Both used federal help to spread ownership.

title: Brown v. Board and Little Rock
objective: After this level you can explain how the NAACP's legal campaign won Brown in 1954, and why integrating schools like Little Rock's was still so hard.
summary: NAACP lawyers built case by case to Brown v. Board (1954): segregated schools are inherently unequal. Delay and resistance, as at Little Rock in 1957, slowed integration.

cards.headline: 1954: “Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”
cards.body: The Supreme Court agreed unanimously. How did lawyers get there, and why was winning only the start?

cards.headline: Start where it’s weakest
cards.body: In the 1930s and 1940s, NAACP lawyers chose their fights. They first attacked “separate but equal” in graduate and law schools, where states rarely had separate Black schools at all. Sweatt v. Painter (1950), a win against a segregated Texas law school, was a major test case in lead lawyer Thurgood Marshall’s strategy. Case by case, they chipped at the wall.

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 58’s “equal protection of the laws,” finally applied to schools.

cards.headline: Brown v. Board
cards.body: Brown v. Board of Education combined five lawsuits from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C. On May 17, 1954, a unanimous Supreme Court ruled that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” violating equal protection. Marshall, the NAACP’s lead counsel, later became a Supreme Court justice himself.

cards.headline: Little Rock
cards.body: In Brown II (1955), the Court told states to desegregate “with all deliberate speed,” a vague phrase many districts used to delay. In September 1957, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock’s Central High. President Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent the 101st Airborne, and the Little Rock Nine entered under escort on September 25, 1957.

cards.headline: Brown and Little Rock: explained
learned: NAACP lawyers began with graduate and law schools
Brown (1954): segregated schools are inherently unequal
Little Rock (1957) needed federal troops to integrate

options.label: Lunch counters in Greensboro

options.label: Graduate and law schools
Interstate bus stations
options.rationale: Bus stations came later, with the Freedom Rides.

options.label: Grade schools in Topeka
options.rationale: Topeka’s grade schools came later, in Brown itself.

options.label: They’re right: schools integrated within weeks
options.rationale: Little Rock was still fighting it in 1957.

options.rationale: The ruling was unanimous.

questions.explanation: Brown was unanimous, but “all deliberate speed” allowed delay, and Little Rock needed federal troops in 1957.

questions.prompt: Level 58’s 14th Amendment bars states from denying “equal protection of the laws.” How did Brown use it?

options.label: It ruled segregated schools violated equal protection
It gave formerly enslaved people citizenship
options.rationale: That was the 14th’s citizenship clause in 1868, not Brown.

options.label: It gave Black men the right to vote
options.rationale: That was the 15th Amendment.

options.label: It ended slavery in the Border States
options.rationale: That was the 13th Amendment.

questions.explanation: Brown held that segregated schools were inherently unequal, violating the 14th Amendment’s equal protection guarantee.

title: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Marches
objective: After this level you can explain how nonviolent direct action, from lunch counters to the March on Washington, pushed the nation to act.
summary: Nonviolent direct action pushed the nation to act: the Greensboro sit-in (1960) and SNCC, CORE’s Freedom Rides (1961) and the March on Washington (1963), followed by the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

cards.headline: Four college freshmen sat down at a whites-only lunch counter.
cards.body: How did ordinary people, protesting without violence, push a whole nation to act?

cards.headline: Sit-ins
cards.body: On February 1, 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T sat at the whites-only Woolworth’s lunch counter in Greensboro. By the end of March, nonviolent sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states. That April, organizer Ella Baker brought student leaders to Raleigh, where they founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, SNCC. Part of that counter now sits in the Smithsonian.

cards.headline: Freedom Rides
cards.body: In Boynton v. Virginia (1960), the Supreme Court banned segregation in bus stations serving interstate travelers, but it went unenforced. So in May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) sent interracial Freedom Riders south on buses to test the ruling. On May 14, near Anniston, Alabama, a mob set their bus on fire with the riders aboard. In September 1961 the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered buses and terminals desegregated.

cards.headline: The March on Washington
cards.body: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, planned by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin. There Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech. The next summer, on July 2, 1964, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, banning segregation in public places.

cards.headline: Nonviolent direct action: explained
learned: Sit-ins spread from Greensboro to 55 cities in 1960
Freedom Riders tested an unenforced ruling in 1961
About 250,000 joined the March on Washington in 1963

options.label: Sue only after moving to another state
options.rationale: The Riders tested segregation where it happened.

options.label: The March on Washington

options.rationale: SNCC was an organization, not a test case.

The Civil Rights Act signing
options.rationale: That was a law being signed.

questions.explanation: Like Plessy, the Freedom Riders rode deliberately to test segregation on interstate travel.

title: The Space Race and the Moon
objective: After this level you can explain why the Soviet Sputnik launch of 1957 set off a space race and how Apollo 11 reached the Moon in 1969.
summary: Sputnik (1957) led to NASA and science funding. After Gagarin’s flight, Kennedy set the Moon goal, and Apollo 11 landed in 1969 amid debate over its cost.

cards.headline: October 4, 1957: a Soviet satellite beeps its way around Earth.
cards.body: Why did one small satellite send the US racing all the way to the Moon?

cards.headline: The Sputnik shock
cards.body: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, which sent out a beeping radio signal. It fed fears that the US had fallen behind in technology, and the Soviets had also tested the first intercontinental ballistic missile that year. The answer came in 1958: President Eisenhower signed the law creating NASA on July 29, and the National Defense Education Act funded schools and colleges so the US could compete in science.

cards.headline: Aim for the Moon
cards.body: The Soviets kept scoring firsts. On April 12, 1961, cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. Six weeks later, on May 25, President John F. Kennedy asked Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out. Getting there took precise math, including that of Katherine Johnson, a Black NASA mathematician who calculated trajectories for Apollo 11.

cards.headline: One small step, one big argument
cards.body: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11’s Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Not everyone thought the race was worth it. As Apollo 11 prepared to launch, Ralph Abernathy led a Poor People’s Campaign protest, with mules and a wagon, to the Kennedy Space Center to point to Americans living in poverty.

cards.headline: The space race: explained
learned: Sputnik (1957) set off fears of falling behind
Congress answered with NASA and science funding
Kennedy’s Moon goal was met by Apollo 11 in 1969

options.label: The first human in space
options.rationale: That was Yuri Gagarin in 1961.

options.label: The first artificial satellite
The first Moon landing craft
options.rationale: That was Apollo 11, an American mission, in 1969.

options.label: The first hydrogen bomb
options.rationale: Sputnik was a satellite, not a weapon.

questions.explanation: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite.

options.rationale: The level shows no Soviet Moon landing.

options.rationale: The protest wasn’t about who flew.

options.label: Gagarin’s goal of orbiting Earth first
options.rationale: Gagarin was Soviet and flew in 1961.

questions.explanation: Kennedy asked in 1961 for a Moon landing before the decade was out; Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969.

title: Vietnam and a Divided Nation
objective: After this level you can explain why the US fought in Vietnam and why the war divided Americans at home.
summary: The domino theory and the Tonkin Resolution drew the US into Vietnam. Tet, the draft and Kent State divided Americans until US forces withdrew in 1973.

cards.headline: More than 58,000 Americans died in Vietnam. At home, the war split the nation.
cards.body: Why did the US fight there, and why couldn’t Americans agree about it?

cards.headline: Falling dominoes
cards.body: In April 1954, President Eisenhower warned that if Indochina fell to communism, its neighbors could fall like dominoes. It was containment, applied to Southeast Asia. In August 1964, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, letting President Lyndon Johnson use force there. The House passed it unanimously, the Senate 88 to 2.

cards.headline: Tet
cards.body: By 1968 the US had more than half a million troops in Vietnam. That January, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched the Tet Offensive. It failed militarily, but its size shook Americans who had been told the war was nearly won.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize every date. Remember the arc: dominoes, escalation, Tet, a divided home front, withdrawal.

cards.headline: Two Americas
cards.body: College deferments let many better-off young men avoid the draft, so most draftees came from poor and working-class families. Protesters marched. On November 3, 1969, President Richard Nixon asked the “great silent majority” to support his war policy. On May 4, 1970, Ohio National Guardsmen fired on antiwar protesters at Kent State University, killing four students.

cards.headline: Getting out
cards.body: The Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 brought a ceasefire and the withdrawal of US forces. The fighting went on without them, and on April 30, 1975, Saigon, South Vietnam’s capital, fell to North Vietnam.

cards.headline: Vietnam: explained
learned: The domino theory drew the US into Vietnam
Tet (1968) shook confidence in the war
The draft and Kent State divided Americans
US troops left after the 1973 Paris accords

options.rationale: That term belongs to a different story.

questions.explanation: Eisenhower’s domino theory held that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors could follow.
