options.rationale: The level mentions no such tax.

questions.explanation: In the Civil War, money bought a way out; in Vietnam, college deferments did much the same, so draftees came mostly from poor and working-class families.

title: The Rights Revolution Spreads
objective: After this level you can explain how women, farmworkers and Native activists built on the civil rights movement, from Title IX to tribal self-government, and why the ERA stalled.
summary: Title IX (1972), farmworkers’ grape contracts (1970) and tribal self-determination (1975) built on civil rights. The ERA passed Congress but fell three states short.

cards.headline: The civil rights movement wrote a playbook. Others picked it up.
cards.body: What did women, farmworkers and Native nations win, and why did one amendment fall short?

cards.headline: Title IX
cards.body: Title IX (1972) says no person shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from any education program receiving federal money. President Richard Nixon signed it on June 23, 1972. One sentence, and every school taking federal dollars had to open its doors to girls and women.

cards.headline: Grapes and a boycott
cards.body: In September 1965, Filipino American grape workers led by Larry Itliong went on strike in Delano, California. Itliong persuaded César Chávez and Dolores Huerta’s mostly Mexican American union to join, and in 1966 the unions merged into what became the United Farm Workers. After a national grape boycott, growers signed contracts in 1970 promising better pay and benefits.

cards.headline: Self-determination
cards.body: In November 1969, activists calling themselves Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island, claiming it as Indian land, and held it for 19 months. In 1970 President Nixon called for “self-determination without termination.” The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975 let tribal governments run their own federal programs.

cards.headline: The ERA stalls
cards.body: Alice Paul wrote the Equal Rights Amendment, first introduced in 1923. It passed Congress in 1972, and 35 of the 38 states needed ratified it. Supporters said it would guarantee that rights could not be denied “on account of sex.” Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA (“Stop Taking Our Privileges”) argued it would take away protections women already had. The deadline, extended to 1982, passed three states short.

cards.headline: The rights revolution: explained
learned: Title IX (1972) barred sex discrimination in schools
Farmworkers won grape contracts in 1970
Tribes won the right to run federal programs (1975)
The ERA fell three states short of ratification

title: Immigration Remade
objective: After this level you can explain how the quotas of 1924 closed the door to most newcomers and how the Immigration Act of 1965 reopened it.
summary: The 1924 quotas favored northern and western Europe and shut out Asia. The 1965 act put family ties and skills first, and newcomers increasingly came from Asia, Africa and Latin America.

cards.headline: 1965: a president signs a law at the Statue of Liberty.
cards.body: He said it was “not a revolutionary bill.” How had the US closed its doors, and how did this law reopen them?

cards.headline: 1924: quotas by nationality
cards.body: The Immigration Act of 1924 set each nationality’s quota at 2 percent of its people in the US in the 1890 census. That formula favored the British Isles and western Europe and limited southern and eastern Europe. The act also barred immigrants “ineligible for citizenship,” cutting off almost all immigration from Asia. Your ancestry decided whether the door opened.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: 1924 sorted newcomers by nationality; 1965 sorted them by family ties and skills.

cards.headline: 1965: family and skills
cards.body: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the national origins quotas. It favored people with family already in the US and skilled workers instead. Who you knew and what you could do now mattered more than where you were born. President Lyndon Johnson signed it on October 3, 1965, at the foot of the Statue of Liberty.

cards.headline: Not revolutionary?
cards.body: At the signing, Johnson said it was “not a revolutionary bill.” Yet after 1965, immigrants came increasingly from Asia, Africa and Latin America rather than Europe. A law about family ties changed which families arrived.

cards.headline: Immigration remade: explained
learned: 1924 quotas favored northern and western Europe
The 1924 act shut out almost all of Asia
1965 favored family ties and skills over nationality

title: Watergate
objective: After this level you can explain how the Watergate scandal led to Nixon's resignation in 1974 and what it changed about how presidents are watched.
summary: A 1972 break-in led to hearings and a secret taping system. The Supreme Court forced out the tapes, Nixon resigned in 1974, and 1978 laws changed how presidents are watched.

cards.headline: June 17, 1972: five burglars caught inside the Democrats’ offices.
cards.body: How did a bungled break-in at the Watergate end a presidency two years later?

cards.headline: Following the trail
cards.body: On June 17, 1972, five burglars were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Washington’s Watergate complex. They were connected to President Richard Nixon’s reelection campaign. Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein kept investigating. Then, on July 16, 1973, at televised Senate hearings, aide Alexander Butterfield revealed a secret White House taping system.

cards.headline: The tapes
cards.body: On July 24, 1974, in United States v. Nixon, the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 0 that Nixon must hand over the tapes. Nixon complied. A tape of June 23, 1972, made public on August 5, caught him trying to halt the FBI’s investigation. His own recorder was the witness.

cards.headline: Resignation
cards.body: In late July 1974 the House Judiciary Committee had approved three articles of impeachment. Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only US president ever to resign. On September 8, President Gerald Ford granted him a full pardon.

cards.headline: New guardrails
cards.body: Congress answered with new rules. The Ethics in Government Act of 1978 required officials to disclose their finances and set up independent counsels to investigate top officials. The Presidential Records Act of 1978 made a president’s official records public property, not private papers.

cards.headline: Watergate: explained
learned: A 1972 break-in was tied to Nixon’s campaign
An 8 to 0 Court forced out the White House tapes
Nixon resigned in 1974, the only president to do so
1978 laws added disclosure and public records

questions.prompt: What did aide Alexander Butterfield reveal at the Senate hearings in July 1973?

options.label: A list of Communists in the government
options.rationale: That was McCarthy’s claim in 1950.

title: Facts and Interpretations
objective: After this level you can tell a historical fact from an interpretation, using historians' rival explanations of why the colonists rebelled.
summary: A fact can be checked; an interpretation argues why. Becker (1909) saw a fight over who should rule at home; Bailyn (1967) saw ideas and a fear of conspiracy against liberty.

cards.headline: Colonists hated the Stamp Act. Why they rebelled is another story.
cards.body: Historians share the same evidence and still disagree. This chapter is about how they argue, starting with the difference between a fact and an interpretation.

cards.headline: What happened, and why
cards.body: Start with something you can check. Remember Level 21? The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed newspapers, legal papers, pamphlets, playing cards and dice. That is a fact: the records prove it. Why colonists went from protesting a tax to fighting a war is an interpretation, an argument built out of facts. The study of how those arguments change over time has a name: historiography, the history of history writing.

cards.headline: Who should rule at home?
cards.body: In 1909 the historian Carl Becker saw two struggles at once. One was over home rule: the colonies against Britain. The other was over who should rule at home: ordinary colonists against their own elite. Progressive historians such as Becker and Charles Beard read the Revolution as a class struggle, and treated the fine speeches about liberty as largely a cover for interests. In their view, interests explained more than speeches.

cards.headline: Take the ideas seriously
cards.body: In 1967 Bernard Bailyn answered from the other side. He studied the pamphlets of the era and took the revolutionaries at their word, assuming people meant what they wrote. In The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, he argued those ideas gave colonists a strong fear of tyranny and of conspiracies against their liberty. That fear, he said, explains why they reacted so hard to Britain’s new policies of the 1760s.

mascot.line: Keep this one: a fact answers what happened. An interpretation answers why, and it is only as strong as its evidence.

cards.headline: Same facts, rival stories
cards.body: Notice what Becker and Bailyn share: the same taxes, protests and pamphlets. They disagree about why people acted. So when you meet a claim about the past, ask one question first. Can I check this, or is someone arguing? Facts get checked. Interpretations get weighed, by how much of the evidence they explain.

title: Reading a Primary Source
objective: After this level you can question a primary source by asking who made it, when, for whom and why, using Frederick Douglass's Fourth of July speech of 1852.
summary: Primary sources come from the time; secondary ones interpret them. Asked who, when, for whom and why, Douglass’s 1852 Rochester speech shows an antislavery audience and a call to the nation.

cards.headline: A famous Fourth of July speech was given on the fifth.
cards.body: In 1852 Frederick Douglass stood before a crowd in Rochester, New York, to talk about Independence Day. To read his words like a historian, you question them first.

cards.headline: Primary or secondary?
cards.body: A primary source is original material made during the time you are studying, by people who lived through it: letters, diaries, official documents. A secondary source, like a history book or a textbook, analyzes and interprets primary sources after the event. Think of a primary source as the witness and a secondary source as the lawyer explaining the case.

cards.headline: Who, when, for whom
cards.body: Historians don’t read a primary source as literal truth. They ask who wrote it, why, and for what audience. Who: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery in 1838 (Level 46). When and where: July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall in Rochester. For whom: he came at the invitation of the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society, and about 500 to 600 people heartily supported his message. A friendly room, not a hostile one.

cards.headline: Why: to rouse a nation
cards.body: Then the why. Douglass asked his listeners, “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?” It is a day, he answered, that reveals “the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” And: “This Fourth [of] July is yours, not mine.” He said outright what he wanted: “the conscience of the nation must be roused.” He was speaking past the room to the whole country.

cards.headline: Read the whole thing
cards.body: A careful reader also notices what surprises. In the same speech Douglass called the signers of the Declaration “brave men.” The Constitution, “interpreted as it ought to be interpreted,” was, he said, “a GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” That fits the reading he adopted in 1851 (Level 33). Quote only the angry lines and you miss his argument: he claimed the nation’s founding promises for the enslaved.

learned: Primary sources come from the time; secondary ones interpret them

Douglass spoke July 5, 1852, to an antislavery audience
He condemned slavery and claimed the Constitution for liberty

title: What Caused the Civil War?
objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on the war's causes, starting with what the seceding states said in their own declarations.
summary: Four seceding states explained themselves in declarations of causes, and Stephens called slavery the Confederacy’s cornerstone. Historians largely consider the Lost Cause false.

cards.headline: Why did the Deep South secede? The people who did it wrote down their answer.
cards.body: After the war, a very different answer spread. Weighing the two is a lesson in how to judge evidence.

cards.headline: Start with their own words
cards.body: Level 51 quoted Mississippi’s blunt line: “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” Mississippi wasn’t alone. Four seceding states, Texas, Mississippi, Georgia and South Carolina, issued declarations of causes explaining why they left the Union, and several named the defense of slavery as their reason. That’s primary evidence, written by the people making the decision, at the moment they made it.

cards.headline: The cornerstone
cards.body: Confederate leaders said the same thing in public. On March 21, 1861, Vice President Alexander Stephens gave what became known as the Cornerstone Speech. The new government’s cornerstone, he said, rested on slavery and on the claim that Black people were not equal to white people. This came from the top, at the start, out loud.

cards.headline: What about states’ rights?
cards.body: South Carolina’s declaration did talk about rights, so look at which ones. It complained that Northern states had passed laws that nullified the federal acts for returning people who escaped slavery, like Level 49’s Fugitive Slave Act, or made them useless. The grievance was that free states used their own powers to shield freedom seekers. As historians point out, the rights in question concerned slavery.

mascot.line: Weigh sources by when they were made: the 1861 declarations outrank memories written after defeat.

cards.headline: The Lost Cause
cards.body: After defeat, a new story took hold. Lost Cause writers claimed secession had little or nothing to do with slavery and was about states’ rights. Historians largely consider the Lost Cause beliefs false, because the evidence from the time of secession, the declarations and speeches above, says otherwise. On this question the evidence is settled.

title: Reconstruction Remembered
objective: After this level you can explain how historians' verdict on Reconstruction changed from the Dunning School to W. E. B. Du Bois and later scholars.
summary: The Dunning School called Reconstruction a mistake. Du Bois’s Black Reconstruction (1935) showed freedpeople shaping it, and revisionists overturned the old verdict.

cards.headline: For decades, many Americans learned that Reconstruction was a tragic mistake.
cards.body: Then historians went back to the evidence and the verdict flipped. How does a whole era get rewritten?

cards.headline: The Dunning School
cards.body: William Archibald Dunning, a Columbia University historian, shaped how Americans understood Reconstruction, through his writings and the many historians he trained. His school called it a mistake. Ill-prepared Black officeholders, it claimed, together with Southern white “scalawags” and Northern “carpetbaggers,” brought havoc on the South.

cards.headline: Du Bois answers
cards.body: In 1935 W. E. B. Du Bois published Black Reconstruction. He showed that freedpeople were not a problem to be managed but actors who shaped Reconstruction’s politics and its gains in civil rights and democracy. Remember Level 59’s evidence: Freedmen’s Bureau schools, Hiram Revels in the Senate, Joseph Rainey in the House. Du Bois put people like them at the center of the story.

cards.headline: The verdict flips
cards.body: Building on the gains of the civil rights movement, revisionist scholars overturned the Dunning School’s picture. Eric Foner of Columbia University sums up the change: Reconstruction, long portrayed as a sordid time, has lately been viewed as a laudable experiment in interracial democracy. Same university as Dunning, opposite verdict.

cards.headline: Not a fairy tale either
cards.body: The newer view doesn’t claim Reconstruction was flawless. Southern Reconstruction governments offered lavish aid to railroads, and that program spawned corruption and rising taxes. The real difference is what gets blamed for its fall. The Dunning School blamed Black officeholders. The evidence of Level 59 points to Klan terror and the withdrawal of federal troops in 1877.

title: Did the New Deal Work?
objective: After this level you can weigh the case that the New Deal rescued the country against the cases that it fell short or went too far.
summary: Output recovered by 1937, but by the standard count unemployment stayed above 10 percent until World War II. The Liberty League said the New Deal did too much; Huey Long said too little.

cards.headline: Did the New Deal work? Americans were arguing about it while it happened.
cards.body: Some said it went too far, others that it didn’t go far enough. Historians still weigh the same record.

cards.headline: The starting line
cards.body: When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed and nearly 25 percent of the labor force was unemployed. Picture one in every four workers with no job to go to. Roosevelt’s answer, the New Deal, poured out programs, some built to last, like Social Security in 1935.

cards.headline: The case that it worked
cards.body: Defenders point to a fast rebound. Richard A. Walker of the Living New Deal writes that by 1937 the recovery had pushed output, income and manufacturing back to 1929 levels. In four years, the economy had climbed out of the hole it fell into after the crash. For its defenders, that is a rescue.

cards.headline: Too far, or not far enough?
cards.body: Critics came from both sides at once. In August 1934 conservatives organized the American Liberty League, arguing Roosevelt had done too much and accusing him of creeping socialism. From the other direction, Senator Huey Long of Louisiana said the New Deal did not do enough. In 1934 he founded the Share Our Wealth Society to limit big fortunes and guarantee every family a minimum.

cards.headline: The fact everyone must explain
cards.body: Here is the stubborn part. By the standard count, which treated workers in federal job programs as unemployed, unemployment stayed above 10 percent through the New Deal years, and only World War II brought full employment. Defenders point to the rebound. Critics on the right say government grew too much; critics on the left say it did too little. Your verdict depends on the yardstick you choose.

title: The Decision to Drop the Bomb
objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments historians make about why the US used atomic bombs on Japan in 1945.
summary: Traditionalists, after Stimson (1947), say the bombs saved lives by avoiding an invasion; revisionists, after Alperovitz (1965), point to the Soviets; many stand between.

cards.headline: Within days of two atomic bombs in 1945, World War II was over. Why use them?
cards.body: Historians agree on what happened that August. They still argue about why it happened.

cards.headline: August 1945
cards.body: On August 6, 1945, the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. On August 9 a second fell on Nagasaki. Estimates of deaths in Hiroshima by the end of 1945 range from 90,000 to 166,000. Japan surrendered within days of the Nagasaki bombing. These facts are not in dispute. The reasons are.

cards.headline: The traditional case
cards.body: The first defense came from inside. In a 1947 Harper’s Magazine article, former Secretary of War Henry Stimson pointed to Japan’s refusal to surrender and the cost of an invasion. Historians called traditionalists agree: the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent an invasion of Japan.

cards.headline: The revisionist case
cards.body: In 1965 historian Gar Alperovitz argued the opposite. Japan, he said, was already close to surrender, so the bombs weren’t needed; they were meant mainly to strengthen the American hand against the Soviet Union. Revisionists point to a real clue: some US policymakers did hope the bomb’s power might push the Soviets to make concessions.

mascot.line: You don’t have to pick a camp today. Practice naming the evidence each side must explain.

cards.headline: Between the poles
cards.body: Many historians take positions between the two camps. J. Samuel Walker, criticizing both, concluded that the main motive was to end the war as quickly as possible. Notice how the argument works: both sides accept the same dates and deaths. They disagree about how close Japan was to surrender and what the decision-makers had in mind.

title: Why the Cold War Ended
objective: After this level you can weigh the explanations for the Cold War's end in 1989 to 1991, from American pressure under Reagan to Gorbachev's reforms and the Soviet economy.
summary: Gorbachev needed to cut military spending; Poland led 1989’s revolutions; the Soviet Union ended in 1991. Historians weigh pressure, protest, reform and economics.

cards.headline: In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell. By the end of 1991 the Soviet Union was gone.
cards.body: Who deserves the credit? Americans, Soviets and Eastern Europeans all tell the story differently, and historians still weigh it.

cards.headline: A new Soviet leader
cards.body: Mikhail Gorbachev became the Soviet leader in March 1985 and inherited a stagnant economy. To restructure it, he needed to reduce military spending at home and political tensions abroad. He and President Ronald Reagan met in four summits between 1985 and 1988. In December 1987 they signed the INF Treaty, which eliminated an entire class of missiles.

cards.headline: The wall comes down
cards.body: Gorbachev loosened Soviet control of Eastern Europe, and people there moved fast. The first revolution of 1989 came in Poland, where the Solidarity movement won freer elections. In November 1989 the Berlin Wall came down, and Communist rule fell across Eastern Europe. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time.

cards.headline: Three kinds of explanation
cards.body: Historians offer rival explanations. Some credit American pressure: Reagan’s military buildup and his Strategic Defense Initiative. Others stress the people of Eastern Europe, especially in Poland, and Soviet overreach in the war in Afghanistan. Still others point to the implosion of the Soviet economy. Each explanation fits some of the evidence.

cards.headline: Weighing them
cards.body: Historians have reached no consensus on how much weight each factor deserves. The State Department’s own historians write that Gorbachev took the initiative in arms control, and that Reagan was well prepared to negotiate. So ask how the causes interact: would pressure have worked without a Soviet leader ready to respond? Would reform have gone so far without people in the streets?

learned: Gorbachev needed to cut military spending to fix the economy
Poland led 1989; the Soviet Union ended in December 1991

title: September 11, 2001
objective: After this level you can describe the attacks of September 11, 2001, and explain why historians treat very recent events differently from the distant past.
summary: On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda hijackers killed 2,977 people. Recent history is harder to judge: records open slowly and verdicts take time.

cards.headline: On one morning in 2001, the United States was attacked at home.
cards.body: It is the most recent event in this tree. Studying it takes the same tools as any other, plus patience.

cards.headline: What happened
cards.body: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 terrorists from al-Qaeda, an Islamist extremist group, hijacked four commercial airplanes. They crashed two into the North and South Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, and a third into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

cards.headline: Flight 93 and the toll
cards.body: On the fourth plane, Flight 93, passengers learned of the other attacks and fought back. The plane crashed into a field in western Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93.

cards.headline: Why recent history is harder
cards.body: Historians of the distant past can read records that were once closed. For recent events, many records are still locked. Under the Presidential Records Act, the public can request a president’s records only five years after the administration ends, and some may be restricted for up to 12 years. The primary sources that explain big decisions arrive slowly.

cards.headline: Give it time
cards.body: Remember Level 64? Matthew Josephson judged the Gilded Age giants in 1934, and Allan Nevins answered him in 1940. Historians can already state what happened on September 11. Why it happened and what it changed will be argued for a long time, as the records open.

cards.headline: September 11, 2001: explained
learned: 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes on 9/11
Flight 93’s passengers fought back; 2,977 people were killed

title: Myths About American History
objective: After this level you can debunk popular myths, like Washington's cherry tree, and explain how such myths get started and why they last.
summary: Weems invented the cherry tree in 1806, Longfellow’s 1860 poem remade Revere’s ride, and the Betsy Ross flag story surfaced in 1870. Myths come late, with a hero and a lesson.

cards.headline: Young George Washington never confessed to chopping down a cherry tree.
cards.body: The story was invented after he died. Myths aren’t just mistakes: someone made each one, for a reason. Finding the maker is how you debunk it.

cards.headline: The parson’s cherry tree
cards.body: Mason Locke “Parson” Weems published his Washington biography in 1800, a year after Washington’s death. The cherry tree story first appeared in its fifth edition, in 1806, six years later. The book became a bestseller, and school readers retold the story to generations of American schoolchildren. A lesson in honesty, made up.

cards.headline: The midnight ride, retold
cards.body: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published “Paul Revere’s Ride” in December 1860, as the crisis between North and South grew. He took significant poetic license. William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode that night. A British patrol stopped all three: Dawes and Prescott escaped, and Revere was held. Revere never reached Concord, and he did not ride alone.

cards.headline: Betsy Ross’s flag
cards.body: The story that Betsy Ross made the first flag was made public by her grandson William Canby in 1870, in a paper to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania drawing on family stories. There is no firm evidence that she designed or made the first flag. She did make flags for the navy. The family story grew into a national legend.

cards.headline: Why myths last
cards.body: Look at the pattern. Each story appeared long after the event, from someone with a reason: a bestselling biographer, a poet in a nation near war, a proud grandson. Each offered a simple hero and a lesson. Level 11 showed another: the 1621 harvest is commonly called the first Thanksgiving, but Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863.

title: Mastery Challenge: US History
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of US History Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: first peoples, colonies, revolution, the republic, a house divided, war and Reconstruction, industry, world power, civil rights and how historians argue.

cards.headline: The US History Mastery Challenge.
